120560.m: Bats also locate prey with the help of the Doppler effect.

120773.q: Which co-receptor marks T helper cells on their surface?
120773.e: Because of their surface molecule CD4, T helper cells are also called CD4-positive T cells. The co-receptor stabilises the binding to the antigen-presenting cell.
120773.m: T helper cells are CD4-positive lymphocytes.

120774.q: Which cells show T helper cells fragments of germs so that they become active?
120774.e: Phagocytes take in germs, break them up and present fragments on their surface. When a T helper cell recognises such a fragment, it is activated.
120774.m: T helper cells are activated by antigen-presenting cells.

120775.q: Which virus specifically attacks T helper cells and, if untreated, leads to AIDS?
120775.e: HIV uses the CD4 molecule as a way in and gradually destroys the T helper cells. Without treatment, the immune defence therefore collapses.
120775.m: HIV weakens the immune system by destroying T helper cells.

120776.q: What role do T helper cells play in making antibodies?
a: They activate B cells, which then make antibodies
They have nothing to do with it
120776.e: B cells usually need the help of T helper cells to develop into plasma cells. Only these then produce large amounts of antibodies.
120776.m: T helper cells help B cells to make antibodies.

120777.q: Why are T helper cells also called the “conductors” of the immune system?
a: They coordinate other defence cells with messenger substances
They carry nerve signals to the brain
120777.e: T helper cells release messenger substances that activate phagocytes, B cells and killer cells. In this way they control the whole defence response.
120777.m: T helper cells control the immune defence.

120778.q: Where do T cells mature, which is also what the “T” in their name refers to?
120778.e: T cells are formed in the bone marrow and then mature in the thymus behind the breastbone. There they learn to tell the body's own substances from foreign ones.
120778.m: T cells mature in the thymus.

120779.q: What is the main job of regulatory T cells?
120779.e: Regulatory T cells slow down immune responses that go too far. In this way they help to prevent autoimmune diseases.
120779.m: Regulatory T cells protect the body from excessive immune reactions.

120780.q: Why do people with untreated AIDS fall ill with infections that are harmless for healthy people?
a: They lack the T helper cells that coordinate the defence
They have too many red blood cells
120780.e: HIV gradually destroys the T helper cells. Without them, the control of the defence collapses, and even otherwise harmless germs become dangerous.
120780.m: Without T helper cells, the defence collapses.

120781.q: What are the messenger substances called that immune cells use to communicate with each other?
120781.e: Cytokines such as the interleukins are released by immune cells. They activate other cells, make them multiply or damp down reactions.

120782.q: To which group of white blood cells do cytotoxic T cells belong?
120782.e: T cells and B cells are lymphocytes and form the specific defence. Granulocytes and monocytes belong to the innate defence.

120784.q: What does a cytotoxic T cell trigger in a cell infected with a virus?
a: Healing of the cell through repair
120784.e: The T cell releases substances that start apoptosis in the target cell. The cell dies in an orderly way, and the viruses inside cannot multiply any further.
120784.m: Cytotoxic T cells make diseased cells destroy themselves.

120785.q: Unlike T cells, which immune cells make antibodies?
120785.e: Activated B cells become plasma cells and release antibodies into the blood. Cytotoxic T cells, on the other hand, kill infected cells directly.

120786.q: Which cells are typically killed by cytotoxic T cells?
a: Cells infected with viruses and tumour cells
120786.e: Cytotoxic T cells recognise foreign peptides on the surface of the body's own cells. In this way they get rid of cells in which viruses are multiplying or that have become abnormal.
120786.m: Cytotoxic T cells remove infected and abnormal body cells.

120787.q: What is the aim of immunotherapy against cancer?
a: To activate the body's own immune system against the tumour
To destroy the tumour with radiation
To remove the tumour by surgery
To switch the immune system off completely
120787.e: Tumours can put the brakes on the defence. Immunotherapies release these brakes or prime T cells specifically so that they attack cancer cells.
120787.m: Immunotherapy turns the body's own defence into a cancer fighter.

120788.q: What is CAR T-cell therapy mainly used for?
a: Against certain types of blood cancer
120788.e: In CAR T-cell therapy, the patient's own T cells are genetically fitted with an artificial receptor. Afterwards they specifically recognise cancer cells, for example in certain leukaemias and lymphomas.
120788.m: CAR T-cell therapy turns your own T cells into targeted cancer hunters.

120789.q: How does a cytotoxic T cell recognise a body cell infected with a virus?
a: By foreign protein fragments on its surface
120789.e: Infected cells show fragments of viral proteins on their surface. The T cell recognises these foreign pieces with its receptor.
120789.m: T cells recognise infected cells by foreign protein fragments.

120790.q: Where do B lymphocytes mature in humans?
120790.e: B lymphocytes form and mature in the bone marrow. T lymphocytes, by contrast, mature in the thymus gland.
120790.m: B cells mature in the bone marrow.

120791.q: Where does the “B” in the name of B lymphocytes originally come from?
a: From the bursa of Fabricius in birds
120791.e: B cells were first discovered in chickens, where they mature in an organ called the bursa of Fabricius. The letter stayed, even though mammals do not have this organ.
120791.m: The “B” of B cells is a reminder of the bursa of Fabricius in birds.

120792.e: The B-cell receptor consists of an antibody anchored in the cell membrane. When it binds its antigen, the B cell is activated.
120792.m: The B-cell receptor is an antibody sitting in the membrane.

120793.q: What does a B cell become after it has recognised its antigen and been activated by a T helper cell?
120793.e: The activated B cell multiplies strongly. Some become plasma cells that make antibodies, others become long-lived memory cells.
120793.m: Activated B cells become plasma cells and memory cells.

120794.q: Why do people usually catch measles only once in their life?
a: The virus dies out after an illness
Afterwards the body makes no more mucous membranes
120794.e: After an infection, memory B cells and memory T cells stay in the body. At the next contact they react so quickly that you no longer fall ill.
120794.m: Memory cells often protect for life.

120795.q: What is the process called in which a B cell switches from making IgM to another antibody class such as IgA or IgE?
120795.e: In class switching, the constant part of the heavy chain is exchanged while the variable part stays the same. So the specificity is kept, but the function of the antibody changes.
120795.m: In class switching, an antibody keeps its target but changes its function.

120796.q: Which antibody class do B cells make first at the first contact with a germ?
120796.e: The early response to a new germ consists mainly of IgM. It is a large pentamer with ten binding sites and is good at clumping germs together.
120796.m: IgM is the first antibody of a new immune response.

120797.q: According to the clonal selection theory, how many different antigen structures is a single naive B cell specific for?
120797.e: Each B cell carries receptors with only one specificity. When it meets its antigen, it multiplies into a clone of identical cells.
120797.m: Each naive B cell recognises only one single antigen structure.

120798.q: Which mechanism creates the enormous variety of antibodies by recombining gene segments?
120798.e: As B cells mature, V, D and J gene segments are randomly put together in new ways. Susumu Tonegawa received the Nobel Prize in 1987 for this discovery.
120798.m: V(D)J recombination creates millions of different antibodies.

120799.q: From which cells do plasma cells develop?
120799.e: Activated B cells divide and develop into plasma cells. These are specialised in producing antibodies.
120799.m: Plasma cells are fully developed B cells.

120800.q: What is the main job of plasma cells?
a: They release large amounts of antibodies
120800.e: Plasma cells are real antibody factories. They release the antibodies into the blood and tissue fluids.
120800.m: Plasma cells produce antibodies in large amounts.

120801.q: Which cell organelle is especially well developed in plasma cells?
120801.e: Antibodies are proteins made for export on the ribosomes of the rough ER. Plasma cells therefore have an extensive rough ER and a large Golgi apparatus.
120801.m: The rough ER is where antibodies are produced in the plasma cell.

120802.q: Besides plasma cells, which cells develop from activated B cells and provide long-lasting immune protection?
120802.e: Some of the activated B cells become memory cells. At a new contact with the germ they react much faster, and this is also how vaccines work.

120803.q: Which cancer starts from abnormal plasma cells in the bone marrow?
120803.e: In multiple myeloma, a single clone of plasma cells multiplies out of control. It often produces large amounts of one uniform antibody and damages the bones.
120803.m: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the plasma cells.

120804.q: Where are long-lived plasma cells mainly found in adults?
a: In the lens of the eye
120804.e: Long-lived plasma cells find special niches with survival signals in the bone marrow. From there they constantly release antibodies into the blood.
120804.m: Long-lived plasma cells live mainly in the bone marrow.

120805.q: What typical shape do the antibodies made by plasma cells have?
120805.e: An antibody consists of four protein chains that together form a Y. With its two arms it binds antigens, for example on germs.

120806.q: Roughly what share of the cells in the bone marrow are plasma cells in healthy adults?
120806.e: Plasma cells are only a small minority in healthy bone marrow. A clearly increased share is a sign of abnormal multiplication.
120806.m: Plasma cells are rare in healthy bone marrow.

120807.q: From which blood cells do macrophages develop?
120807.e: Monocytes circulate in the blood and move into tissues. There they mature into macrophages.
120807.m: Macrophages develop from monocytes in the blood.

120808.q: What does the Greek word “macrophage” mean?
120808.e: The word comes from the Greek “makros” for big and “phagein” for to eat. It describes the ability to take in large particles.
120808.m: Macrophages are the body's big eating cells.

120810.q: Which structure do macrophages form in tuberculosis to wall in germs?
120810.e: In tuberculosis, macrophages, giant cells and lymphocytes gather in small nodules around the bacteria. In this way the germs are walled in, but often not completely killed.
120810.m: Macrophages wall in tuberculosis bacteria in granulomas.

120811.q: How do macrophages recognise bacteria without having met them before?
a: By typical molecular patterns on the bacterial surface
By antibodies that they make themselves
120811.e: Receptors such as the Toll-like receptors recognise building blocks common to many germs, such as lipopolysaccharide. This is part of the innate defence.
120811.m: Macrophages recognise typical molecular patterns of germs.

120812.q: Apart from eating germs, what job do macrophages have?
a: They clear away cell debris and help wounds heal
120812.e: Depending on the signals, macrophages act more to promote inflammation (M1) or more to heal (M2). M2 macrophages clean up and promote the building of tissue.
120812.m: Macrophages fight germs and help with healing.

120813.q: Which macrophages clear away inhaled dust particles in the air sacs of the lungs?
120813.e: Alveolar macrophages move along the inner surface of the air sacs. They take in dust, soot and germs and are therefore also called dust cells.
120813.m: Alveolar macrophages keep the air sacs of the lungs clean.

120814.q: Which cells in the spleen mainly break down old red blood cells?
120814.e: Red blood cells live for about 120 days and then become less flexible. Macrophages in the spleen recognise and digest them, and the iron is recycled.
120814.m: Macrophages in the spleen dispose of old red blood cells.

120815.q: What, among other things, do macrophages use to kill bacteria they have taken in, inside the phagolysosome?
120815.e: An enzyme complex in the membrane produces superoxide and other aggressive oxygen compounds in the so-called respiratory burst. Together with enzymes and acid, they destroy the bacteria.
120815.m: Macrophages kill bacteria with aggressive oxygen compounds.

120816.q: Which part of the immune system does the complement system mainly belong to?
120816.e: The complement system consists of over 30 proteins in the blood plasma that can be activated without prior learning. But it works closely with antibodies.
120816.m: The complement system is part of the innate defence.

120817.q: With which part of the acquired defence does the complement system work closely?
120817.e: When antibodies stick to a germ, they can activate the complement system. This so-called classical pathway links the acquired defence with the innate defence.
120817.m: Antibodies can switch on the complement system.

120818.q: What does the complement system mainly consist of?
120818.e: The complement system includes over 30 proteins dissolved in the blood. They activate each other as in a cascade; one central protein is called C3.
120818.m: The complement system is a cascade of blood proteins.

120819.q: How does the complement system directly kill bacteria at the end of its cascade?
a: It makes holes in their membrane
It breaks them down with stomach acid
120819.e: Several complement proteins join together to form the membrane attack complex. Water flows in through this pore, and the bacterial cell bursts.
120819.m: The membrane attack complex punches holes in bacteria.

120820.q: What is it called when germs are marked with proteins such as C3b so that phagocytes can take them in more easily?
120820.e: C3b sticks to the surface of the germ. Phagocytes have receptors for it and therefore recognise marked germs much better.

120821.q: What effect do small fragments of the complement system such as C3a and C5a have?
120821.e: C3a and C5a widen blood vessels and attract immune cells. They are called anaphylatoxins; in large amounts they can contribute to shock.

120822.q: Why does the complement system have this name?
a: Because it complements the effect of antibodies
Because it is made of complex sugars
Because it only attacks complete cells
120822.e: At the end of the 19th century it was noticed that antibodies only dissolve bacteria together with a heat-sensitive factor in the serum. This complementing factor was therefore called “complement”.
120822.m: Complement adds to the effect of antibodies.

120823.q: Which symptoms typically occur in attacks in hereditary angioedema?
a: Severe swelling of the skin and mucous membranes
120823.e: In hereditary angioedema, a braking protein of the complement system, the C1 esterase inhibitor, is missing. Swellings develop that can become life-threatening in the larynx.
120823.m: In hereditary angioedema, the skin and mucous membranes swell up.

120824.q: What is the major histocompatibility complex also called in humans?
120824.e: In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens, HLA for short. They were first detected on white blood cells.
120824.m: The human MHC is called the HLA system.

120825.q: What are MHC molecules on the surface of body cells for?
a: They show the immune system fragments of proteins
120825.e: MHC molecules present small pieces of proteins. T cells check these and so recognise whether a cell is infected or foreign.
120825.m: MHC molecules show the immune system what is inside a cell.

120826.q: Which cells carry MHC class I molecules?
a: Almost all body cells with a nucleus
120826.e: MHC class I molecules show fragments of proteins made inside the cell itself. Because almost every cell with a nucleus carries them, the immune system can detect infections almost everywhere.
120826.m: Almost every cell with a nucleus shows on MHC class I molecules what is going on inside it.

120827.q: What is HLA typing used for before a blood stem cell transplant?
a: To find the best possible matching donor
To determine the ABO blood group
120827.e: The better the HLA features match, the lower the risk of rejection and graft-versus-host disease. In Switzerland, Blood Transfusion Service SRC Switzerland keeps the register of blood stem cell donors.
120827.m: Matching HLA features are crucial for a stem cell transplant.

120828.q: Which feature of the HLA genes makes it hard to find a suitable unrelated donor?
a: Their position on the Y chromosome
120828.e: The HLA genes are among the most varied human genes, with thousands of known variants. That is why siblings are often a better match than unrelated people.
120828.m: HLA genes are extremely varied, which makes the search for a donor harder.

120829.q: What does the term histocompatibility mean?
120829.e: Histo means tissue, compatible means able to go together. The better the features of donor and recipient match, the better a transplant is tolerated.

120830.q: What can happen if the HLA features of a transplanted organ match the recipient poorly?
a: The immune system rejects the organ
The organ grows twice as fast
The organ becomes invisible to the immune system
120830.e: The immune system recognises foreign HLA features and attacks the organ. That is why matching donors are sought and medicines are given that damp down the immune system.
120830.m: Poorly matching HLA features lead to rejection.

120831.q: Which Swiss scientist shared the 1996 Nobel Prize with Peter Doherty for discovering that T cells only recognise antigens together with the body's own MHC molecules?
120831.e: Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty showed that cytotoxic T cells only kill virus-infected cells if these carry the matching MHC molecules. This principle is called MHC restriction.
120831.m: Rolf Zinkernagel discovered MHC restriction with Peter Doherty.

a: Messenger substances for communication between cells
Building blocks of the cell membrane
120832.e: Cytokines are small proteins that cells release to influence other cells. They control growth, inflammation and immune responses.
120832.m: Cytokines are the messenger substances of the immune system.

120833.q: How is fever useful during an infection?
a: It supports the defence and slows down many germs
120833.e: Cytokines turn up the set point for body temperature in the brain. The higher temperature makes immune cells more active and slows the multiplying of many germs.
120833.m: Fever helps the body fight germs.

120834.q: What is a life-threatening, excessive release of cytokines called?
120834.e: In a cytokine storm, immune cells release large amounts of messenger substances out of control. This can lead to high fever, circulatory failure and organ damage.
120834.m: A cytokine storm is a dangerous overreaction of the immune system.

120835.q: For which kind of illness are medicines used that block inflammation-promoting cytokines?
120835.e: In diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Crohn's disease, cytokines constantly drive the inflammation. Blocking them calms the inflammation down.
120835.m: Cytokine blockers slow down chronic inflammation.

120836.q: What are cytokines called that lure immune cells to a particular place?
120836.e: Chemokines form a concentration gradient that immune cells follow. This directed movement is called chemotaxis.
120836.m: Chemokines show immune cells the way.

120837.q: What does the name “interleukin” literally mean?
120837.e: The name came about because these messenger substances were first recognised as signals between white blood cells. Today we know that other cells make them too.
120837.m: Interleukins pass on signals between leukocytes.

120838.q: Which signs of inflammation are partly triggered by cytokines?
120838.e: Cytokines widen blood vessels and attract immune cells. As a result, the area becomes red, warm, swollen and painful.
120838.m: Cytokines help trigger the typical signs of inflammation.

120839.q: Where are white blood cells made?
120839.e: In the red bone marrow, all blood cells develop from stem cells. Cytokines such as growth factors control how many white blood cells are made.
120839.m: White blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

120840.q: Where do interferons get their name from?
a: Because they interfere with the multiplying of viruses
Because they develop in the inner ear
120840.e: The name comes from “interference”. Interferons slow down the multiplying of viruses in cells.
120840.m: Interferons interfere with the multiplying of viruses.

120841.q: Which Swiss researcher discovered interferons together with Alick Isaacs in 1957?
120841.e: In London, Jean Lindenmann and Alick Isaacs observed that cells treated with a virus release a substance that protects other cells from viruses. Lindenmann later became a professor at the University of Zurich.
120841.m: Jean Lindenmann was a co-discoverer of interferons.

120842.q: Which body cells can make interferon alpha and beta when they are attacked by a virus?
120842.e: Interferon alpha and beta belong to type I. Almost every body cell can make them as soon as it detects viral genetic material, and so it warns its neighbouring cells.
120842.m: Virus-infected cells release interferon alpha and beta.

120843.q: Which phagocytes are activated especially strongly by interferon gamma?
120843.e: Interferon gamma comes mainly from T cells and natural killer cells. It helps macrophages to kill the germs they have taken in more effectively.

120844.q: For which disease is interferon beta used as a long-term treatment?
120844.e: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, interferon beta can reduce the number of relapses. It was one of the first medicines that influence the course of this disease.
120844.m: Interferon beta is used for multiple sclerosis.

120845.q: For which viral infection was interferon alpha the standard treatment for a long time, before directly acting drugs arrived?
120845.e: Interferon alpha was usually given together with ribavirin for many months and had strong side effects. Today, directly acting antiviral tablets cure hepatitis C in most cases.
120845.m: Hepatitis C used to be treated with interferon alpha.

120846.q: How do type I interferons protect neighbouring cells from viruses?
a: They trigger the making of antiviral proteins there
They destroy viruses directly in the blood
120846.e: Interferons bind to receptors on neighbouring cells and switch on many genes there. The resulting proteins slow down, for example, the protein production of the viruses.
120846.m: Interferons put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state.

120847.q: Which side effect is especially common with interferon treatment?
120847.e: Interferons trigger the same signals as a viral infection. That is why people being treated often suffer from fever, aching limbs and tiredness.
120847.m: Interferons often cause flu-like side effects.

120848.q: Which cells make sure the body reacts faster at a second contact with a germ?
120848.e: After an infection, specific memory B and T cells remain. They recognise the germ again and quickly trigger a strong response.
120848.m: Memory cells remember germs that were fought before.

120849.q: Which antibody class dominates in the secondary response to a known germ?
120849.e: Memory B cells have usually already gone through class switching. In the secondary response, large amounts of high-affinity IgG antibodies are therefore made quickly.
120849.m: IgG antibodies dominate in the secondary response.

120850.q: What is a vaccination called in which the body makes antibodies and memory cells itself?
120850.e: In active immunisation, the body receives weakened or killed germs or parts of them. The immune system reacts and builds up a memory.
120850.m: In active immunisation, the immune system learns for itself.

120851.q: Why does passive immunisation not leave long-lasting protection?
a: It only works in the gut
120851.e: In passive immunisation, you receive ready-made antibodies, for example against tetanus. These are broken down after a few weeks, and no memory cells of your own are formed.
120851.m: Passive immunisation protects at once, but only for a short time.

120852.q: How does the secondary response differ in timing from the primary response?
120852.e: In the primary response it usually takes one to two weeks until there are many antibodies. In the secondary response a few days are enough, because memory cells are already waiting.
120852.m: The secondary response is faster and stronger than the primary response.

120853.q: Why does a measles vaccination usually protect for life, but a flu vaccination only for one season?
a: Flu viruses have no surface proteins
The flu vaccine contains no antigens
120853.e: Memory cells recognise a virus by its surface structures. In the measles virus these stay stable, while flu viruses keep changing them.
120853.m: Stable viruses allow a long immune memory.

120854.q: What is the indirect protection of unvaccinated people called when a large part of the population is immune?
120854.e: If the majority is immune, a germ hardly finds new hosts and does not spread. In this way people who cannot be vaccinated are also protected.
120854.m: Herd immunity also protects those who are not immune themselves.

120855.q: Why is a new flu vaccination needed almost every year despite immune memory?
a: The virus's surface proteins keep changing
Memory cells only live for one day
The vaccine only works in summer
120855.e: Through mutations, the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase of influenza viruses constantly change. This process is called antigenic drift, and the old antibodies then fit less well.
120855.m: Because of antigenic drift, the flu vaccine has to be updated regularly.

120856.e: Immunosuppression means that the defence is weakened, either on purpose or by disease. Doctors use it for transplants and autoimmune diseases.

120857.q: Why do people have to take immunosuppressants after an organ transplant?
a: So that the donor organ is not rejected
So that the organ grows faster
So that they do not get allergies
So that the blood becomes thicker
120857.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ by its HLA features and would attack it. Immunosuppressants prevent this rejection reaction.
120857.m: Immunosuppressants protect a donor organ from rejection.

120858.q: Which important immunosuppressant was discovered at Sandoz in Basel in the 1970s?
120858.e: Ciclosporin comes from a soil fungus and was studied by researchers around Jean-François Borel at Sandoz. It made organ transplants much more successful.
120858.m: Ciclosporin from Basel revolutionised transplant medicine.

120859.q: Which immune cells mainly attack a donor organ during rejection?
120859.e: T cells recognise the foreign HLA features of the donor organ and attack it. Medicines such as ciclosporin and tacrolimus slow down their activation.
120859.m: During rejection, mainly T cells attack the donor organ.

120860.q: Which group of steroid hormones is often used to suppress inflammation and immune reactions?
120860.e: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone block the production of many inflammatory messenger substances. They are used, for example, for asthma, rheumatism and severe allergies.
120860.m: Glucocorticoids damp down inflammation and immune reactions.

120861.q: Which risk rises especially with long-term immunosuppression?
a: Blood sugar too high because of viruses
120861.e: Opportunistic germs are usually harmless for healthy people but can cause serious illness when the defence is weakened. Certain types of cancer also become more common.
120861.m: People who are immunosuppressed are especially prone to infections.

120862.q: What are diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis called, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissue?
120862.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the inner lining of the joints. It is treated with medicines that damp down the immune system, such as methotrexate.
120862.m: In autoimmune diseases, the defence attacks the body itself.

120863.q: Why does chemotherapy often weaken the immune defence?
a: It damages fast-dividing cells in the bone marrow
It thins the blood with water
120863.e: Cytostatic drugs attack all rapidly dividing cells, including the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. As a result, the number of white blood cells drops for a while.
120863.m: Chemotherapy weakens the defence because it hits the bone marrow.

120864.q: Which cells are most effective at activating naive T cells for the first time?
120864.e: Dendritic cells take up antigens in the tissue and present them in the lymph nodes. They carry especially many MHC and co-stimulatory molecules.
120864.m: Dendritic cells are the best starter cells for the T-cell response.

120865.q: What does a body cell infected with a virus show on its surface?
120865.e: Infected cells present pieces of the viral proteins on special molecules, the MHC molecules. In this way T cells can recognise that the cell is infected.
120865.m: Infected cells show the immune system fragments of the virus.

120866.q: Which T cells kill virus-infected cells that present a foreign antigen to them?
120866.e: Cytotoxic T cells, also called killer cells, recognise fragments of virus on the surface of infected cells. They then trigger the death of these cells.
120866.m: Killer T cells remove infected body cells.

120867.q: Why do T cells only recognise an antigen when another cell presents it to them?
a: Their receptor only binds fragments on MHC molecules
They have no receptors at all
They can only bind whole bacteria
120867.e: Unlike B cells, T cells do not recognise free germs. Their receptor only fits peptide pieces lying on the MHC molecules of a cell.
120867.m: T cells need a presented antigen.

120868.q: How do macrophages and dendritic cells take in whole bacteria before presenting parts of them?
120868.e: In phagocytosis, the cell flows around the bacterium with its membrane and digests it in a small vesicle. It then presents fragments of it on its surface.

120869.q: Which cells, once activated by an antigen-presenting cell, help B cells to make antibodies?
120869.e: T helper cells recognise a presented antigen and then release signals and messenger substances. In this way they stimulate matching B cells to make antibodies.
120869.m: T helper cells coordinate the immune response.

120870.q: What happens when a naive T cell recognises its antigen without a co-stimulatory signal?
120870.e: Without a second signal, the T cell switches into a state of unresponsiveness, called anergy. This protects against attacks on the body's own structures.
120870.m: Without co-stimulation, a T cell stays silent.

120871.q: Where do dendritic cells travel after taking up an antigen in the tissue?
120871.e: Through the lymph vessels, the dendritic cells reach the lymph node. There they meet many naive T cells and can activate the matching one.
120871.m: Dendritic cells carry antigens to the lymph nodes.

120872.q: Where do dendritic cells get their name from?
a: From being found in the teeth
120872.e: The Greek word dendron means tree. The cells have many tree-like branching extensions with which they capture and present antigens.
120872.m: Dendritic cells are named after their tree-like projections.

121169.q: What does a live vaccine contain?
a: Weakened germs that can still multiply
Only individual proteins of the germ
121169.e: Live vaccines contain germs that can still multiply but are weakened so much that they normally do not cause the disease. The body reacts much as it would to a real infection.
121169.m: A live vaccine contains weakened germs that can still multiply.

121170.q: What is the deliberate weakening of a germ for a live vaccine called?
121170.e: In attenuation, a germ loses its ability to cause disease, for example through many passages in cell cultures. Its ability to trigger an immune response is kept.
121170.m: Attenuated germs are weakened but still trigger an immune response.

121171.q: Which combination vaccine is made of live vaccines?
121171.e: The MMR vaccine contains weakened measles, mumps and rubella viruses. The vaccines against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and hepatitis, by contrast, are inactivated vaccines.
121171.m: The MMR vaccination is a live vaccination.

121172.q: For which group of people are live vaccines generally not suitable?
a: People with a severe immune deficiency
People with a mild cold without fever
121172.e: With a severe immune deficiency, the weakened germ can multiply out of control and cause illness. That is why live vaccines are then usually not allowed; they are also not given during pregnancy.
121172.m: With a severe immune deficiency, live vaccines are avoided.

121173.q: What gap is recommended if two live vaccines are not given on the same day?
121173.e: Two live vaccines are given either at the same time or at least four weeks apart. Otherwise the reaction to the first vaccination could weaken the effect of the second.
121173.m: Two live vaccines are given together or four weeks apart.

121174.q: Which vaccine against tuberculosis is a live vaccine with weakened cattle tuberculosis bacteria?
121174.e: BCG stands for Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis. In Switzerland, BCG vaccination is now only used in special situations.
121174.m: The BCG vaccine against tuberculosis is a live vaccine.

121175.q: Why are one or two doses of a live vaccine often enough for long protection?
a: The germs multiply and imitate a real infection
They contain especially much aluminium as a booster
They are injected directly into the bloodstream
They contain ready-made antibodies from donor blood
121175.e: Because the weakened germs multiply in the body, the immune response is strong and wide-ranging, including T cells. This often gives long-lasting protection.
121175.m: Live vaccines imitate an infection and often protect for a long time.

121176.q: Which scientist developed a vaccine against rabies with a weakened germ in 1885?
121176.e: Louis Pasteur weakened the rabies germ in dried spinal cord from rabbits. In 1885 he used it to successfully treat Joseph Meister, a boy who had been bitten.
121176.m: Louis Pasteur developed the rabies vaccine in 1885.

121177.q: What is the hallmark of an inactivated vaccine?
a: It contains no germs that can multiply
It only works through the mucous membranes
121177.e: Inactivated vaccines contain killed germs, parts of them or toxins made harmless. They cannot multiply in the body and therefore cannot cause the disease.
121177.m: An inactivated vaccine cannot multiply in the body.

121178.q: What is a toxoid, as used in the tetanus vaccine?
a: A bacterial toxin that has been made harmless
An artificial mRNA for the toxin
121178.e: In a toxoid, the toxin, such as tetanus toxin, is detoxified chemically, for example with formaldehyde. But it keeps its structure, so the body makes antibodies against it.
121178.m: A toxoid is a detoxified bacterial toxin that still creates immunity.

121179.q: Which of these vaccinations is a toxoid vaccination?
121179.e: In diphtheria it is not the bacterium itself but its toxin that makes you ill. That is why diphtheria toxoid is used for vaccination; measles, yellow fever and chickenpox are live vaccinations.

121180.q: Why do inactivated vaccines usually need several doses for the primary course?
a: Without multiplying, they trigger a weaker immune response
They are excreted from the body at once
They only contain antibodies without memory
They only work after a year
121180.e: Because the antigens do not multiply, the stimulus for the immune system is weaker. Several doses and later boosters build up stable protection.
121180.m: Inactivated vaccines usually need several doses.

121181.q: How is the hepatitis B vaccine made today?
a: By genetic engineering in yeast cells, as a surface protein
121181.e: The vaccine contains the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), which is produced by genetic engineering, usually in yeast cells. It contains no complete viruses and therefore cannot cause an infection.
121181.m: The hepatitis B vaccine contains a genetically engineered virus protein.

121182.q: What are inactivated vaccines called that contain only individual, purified parts of the germ?
121182.e: Subunit vaccines contain only selected antigens, such as surface proteins. This makes them well tolerated, but they often need adjuvants.
121182.m: Subunit vaccines contain only selected parts of a germ.

121183.q: Which advantage of inactivated vaccines is important for people with an immune deficiency?
a: They work without any side effects
They protect against all germs at once
121183.e: Because inactivated vaccines contain no germs that can multiply, they are safe even when the immune system is weakened. The protection may then be weaker, however.
121183.m: Inactivated vaccines are safe even with an immune deficiency.

121184.q: Against which tick-borne disease in Switzerland is an inactivated vaccine used?
121184.e: The TBE vaccine contains inactivated viruses. The Federal Office of Public Health recommends it in almost all of Switzerland because infected ticks are widespread.
121184.m: An inactivated vaccine protects against TBE.

121185.q: What gets into the body cells with an mRNA vaccine against Covid-19?
a: Building instructions for the spike protein
A piece of DNA that is built into the genome
121185.e: The mRNA contains the blueprint for the spike protein of the virus. The cells make this protein for a short time, and the immune system learns to recognise it.
121185.m: The mRNA delivers the blueprint for a virus protein.

121186.q: Where in the cell is the vaccine mRNA translated into protein?
a: At the ribosomes in the cytoplasm
In the cell nucleus at the DNA
121186.e: The mRNA stays in the cytoplasm and is read there by ribosomes. It does not get into the cell nucleus and does not change the DNA.
121186.m: Vaccine mRNA is read at ribosomes in the cytoplasm.

121187.q: What are lipid nanoparticles in mRNA vaccines for?
a: They protect the mRNA and bring it into the cells
They kill the viruses in the blood
They colour the injection site so it can be seen
121187.e: Free mRNA would be broken down quickly. Tiny fat shells, the lipid nanoparticles, protect it and merge with the cell membrane.
121187.m: Lipid nanoparticles package the delicate mRNA.

121188.q: What happens to the vaccine mRNA after a few days?
a: It is broken down by the cell
It is permanently built into the genome
121188.e: mRNA is a short-lived molecule and is broken down by the cell's own enzymes. What remains is the immune memory.
121188.m: Vaccine mRNA is broken down after a short time.

121189.q: Who received the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that made mRNA vaccines possible?
121189.e: Karikó and Weissman discovered that modified nucleosides make mRNA cause less inflammation. This base modification was crucial for effective mRNA vaccines.
121189.m: Karikó and Weissman received the 2023 Nobel Prize for mRNA research.

121190.q: Why can mRNA vaccines be adapted to new virus variants relatively quickly?
a: You only have to change the building instructions in the mRNA
New viruses have to be grown in hens' eggs
The mRNA adapts itself in the body
You only have to increase the dose
121190.e: Once the genome of a new variant is known, the building instructions for its spike protein are written into the mRNA. Otherwise production stays the same.
121190.m: With mRNA vaccines, only the building instructions are swapped.

121191.q: In which year was the first mRNA vaccine against Covid-19 approved in Switzerland?
121191.e: The vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech was approved in December 2020. It was the first Covid-19 vaccine approved in Switzerland.
121191.m: The first mRNA vaccine was approved in Switzerland in December 2020.

121192.q: What practical drawback did the first mRNA vaccines against Covid-19 have?
a: They had to be stored deep-frozen
They had to be injected into a vein
They were only approved for children
They could only be given as a tablet
121192.e: mRNA is unstable, so the vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech, for example, at first had to be stored at around minus 70 degrees Celsius. This made distribution harder.
121192.m: Early mRNA vaccines needed very cold storage.

121193.q: From which Latin word does “adjuvant” come?
121193.e: “Adiuvare” means to help or support. The adjuvant helps the antigen to trigger a strong immune response.
121193.m: An adjuvant is a helper for the immune system.

121194.q: Which adjuvants have been used most often in vaccines for almost 100 years?
121194.e: Aluminium hydroxide and aluminium phosphate have been used since the 1920s and 1930s, for example in tetanus and diphtheria vaccines. The amount per dose is very small.
121194.m: Aluminium salts are the oldest and most common adjuvants.

121195.q: Which type of vaccine usually needs no adjuvant?
121195.e: Live vaccines already trigger a strong immune response because the germs multiply. Inactivated vaccines, especially subunit and toxoid vaccines, on the other hand often need adjuvants.
121195.m: Live vaccines usually manage without an adjuvant.

121196.q: Which advantage of an adjuvant is important when vaccines are scarce, for example in a flu pandemic?
a: Less antigen is needed per dose
The vaccine is cheaper to transport
121196.e: With an adjuvant, a smaller amount of antigen is often enough for the same protection. In this way more doses can be made from the same production.

121197.q: Why is an adjuvant added to a vaccine?
121197.e: An adjuvant is an enhancer. It makes the immune system react more strongly to the antigen.
121197.m: An adjuvant strengthens the effect of a vaccination.

121198.q: Which side effect occurs more often with adjuvanted vaccines?
a: Redness and pain at the injection site
Loss of the sense of taste
121198.e: Because adjuvants stimulate a local inflammatory reaction, pain, redness or swelling at the injection site happen more often. These reactions usually fade after a few days.
121198.m: Adjuvants can irritate the injection site more.

121199.q: Which part of the vaccine is the antigen against which the body forms its defence?
121199.e: The antigen is a part of the germ or the weakened germ itself. The immune system learns to recognise it; the adjuvant only strengthens this reaction.
121199.m: The body forms its defence against the antigen.

121200.q: Why does a booster vaccination work faster and more strongly than the first vaccination?
a: The vaccine is twice as strong
The immune system is older by then
121200.e: After the primary course, memory B cells and memory T cells remain. At the booster they multiply quickly, and a strong secondary response develops.
121200.m: A booster wakes up the immune memory.

121201.q: Which antibody class dominates in the secondary response after a booster?
121201.e: In the first response, mainly IgM antibodies are made at first. In the secondary response, IgG antibodies with high binding strength dominate.

121202.q: What is the process called in which antibodies bind better and better after repeated contact with the antigen?
121202.e: In the germinal centres of the lymph nodes, B cells with especially well-binding antibodies are selected. As a result, the affinity of the antibodies rises after each booster.
121202.m: Through affinity maturation, antibodies bind better and better.

121203.q: At what intervals is the tetanus booster recommended in Switzerland for adults between 25 and 65?
121203.e: The Swiss vaccination schedule provides boosters at 25, 45 and 65. From 65, a booster is given every 10 years, as the immune response becomes weaker in old age.
121203.m: In Switzerland, adults up to 65 have a tetanus booster every 20 years.

121204.q: How often is a booster against TBE recommended in Switzerland?
121204.e: After the primary course of three doses, the TBE vaccination in Switzerland is boosted every 10 years. This applies to people who spend time in risk areas.
121204.m: The TBE vaccination is boosted every 10 years.

121205.q: Why is the flu vaccination given anew every year?
a: Flu viruses keep changing their surface proteins
The vaccine only works for one month
The memory cells die every winter
121205.e: Through antigenic drift, the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase of flu viruses constantly change. That is why the vaccine is adapted every year to the virus strains expected.
121205.m: Flu vaccines are adapted every year because of antigenic drift.

121206.q: What is the gradual fading of vaccine protection over time called?
121206.e: With some vaccinations, the antibody level drops over time and protection fades. Boosters make up for this effect.
121206.m: Fading vaccine protection is called waning immunity.

121207.q: What is the series of vaccinations called that builds up the first protection before later boosters?
121207.e: The primary course usually consists of several doses weeks or months apart. Only on top of this does the booster extend protection for years.
121207.m: The primary course comes before the booster.

121208.q: What does the basic reproduction number R0 tell you?
a: How many people one infected person infects on average when everyone is susceptible
How many people die of a disease
How long the incubation period lasts
How many people are already vaccinated
121208.e: R0 describes the average number of further infections caused by one case in a completely unprotected population. If R0 is greater than 1, a disease can spread.
121208.m: R0 counts infections per case in an unprotected population.

121209.q: A disease has an R0 of 4. What share of the population must at least be immune so that it no longer spreads?
121209.e: The threshold for herd immunity is 1 minus 1/R0. With R0 equal to 4, this gives 1 minus 0.25, which is 0.75, so 75 %.
121209.m: The herd immunity threshold is 1 minus 1 divided by R0.

121210.q: Which disease has one of the highest basic reproduction numbers, with an R0 of about 12 to 18?
121210.e: Measles is extremely contagious and spreads through the air. That is why herd protection needs a very high share of immune people.
121210.m: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases of all.

121211.q: Why does tetanus not have a meaningful basic reproduction number?
a: Tetanus is not passed from person to person
Tetanus is only spread by mosquitoes
121211.e: Tetanus spores get into wounds from the environment, for example from soil. As no person infects another, there is no herd immunity; everyone has to protect themselves by vaccination.
121211.m: Only your own vaccination protects you against tetanus.

121212.q: How is the effective reproduction number R related to R0 when a share s of the population is still susceptible?
a: R equals R0 divided by s
121212.e: The fewer people are still susceptible, the fewer infections succeed. With R0 equal to 3 and s equal to 0.5, R becomes 1.5.
121212.m: The effective reproduction number is R0 times the share of susceptible people.

121213.q: An infection has an R0 of 3. Without countermeasures, how many new infections arise from a single case in the fourth generation of infection?
121213.e: Each generation triples the number: 3, 9, 27, 81. In the fourth generation, there are therefore 3 to the power of 4, which is 81 new cases.
121213.m: If R0 is greater than 1, case numbers grow exponentially.

121214.q: Which value of the effective reproduction number means that an epidemic is dying down?
121214.e: If each case infects fewer than one other person on average, the number of new infections falls from generation to generation. At exactly 1, it stays roughly constant.
121214.m: An epidemic dies down when R is below 1.

121215.q: Which three quantities determine R0 in a simple model?
a: Contact rate, probability of transmission and length of infectiousness
Vaccination rate, death rate and age
121215.e: R0 is roughly the product of the number of contacts per day, the probability of infection per contact and the number of infectious days. Measures such as keeping a distance or isolation reduce these factors.
121215.m: R0 depends on contacts, transmission and how long someone is infectious.

121216.q: A disease has an R0 of 5 and the vaccine protects 90 % of those vaccinated. Roughly what vaccination rate is needed for herd protection?
121216.e: The threshold is 1 minus 1/5, which is 0.8. Because only 90 % of those vaccinated are protected, you need 0.8 divided by 0.9, which is around 0.89 or 89 %.
121216.m: If a vaccine is not fully effective, a higher vaccination rate is needed.

121217.q: What does the vaccination coverage rate describe?
a: The share of a population group that has received a certain vaccination
The number of vaccine doses made per year
How effective a vaccine is in the laboratory
The number of vaccination centres per canton
121217.e: The vaccination coverage rate shows what percentage of a group is vaccinated. It is often recorded separately by age and vaccine dose.
121217.m: The vaccination coverage rate is the share of vaccinated people in a group.

121218.q: At a school, 552 of 600 young people have had two doses of measles vaccine. What is the vaccination coverage rate?
121218.e: 552 divided by 600 gives 0.92. The vaccination coverage rate is therefore 92 %.
121218.m: The coverage rate is calculated as vaccinated people divided by the total number.

121219.q: What two-dose vaccination coverage rate does the WHO recommend to eliminate measles?
121219.e: Because measles is so contagious, at least 95 % of people need to be immune. Only then can chains of infection be reliably broken.

121220.q: In which age groups does Switzerland regularly record vaccination coverage in the cantons?
121220.e: The Swiss vaccination coverage monitoring checks the vaccination records of 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds. The data are published by the Federal Office of Public Health.
121220.m: In Switzerland, vaccination coverage is recorded for 2-, 8- and 16-year-olds.

121221.q: Why does a high vaccination coverage rate also protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
a: Because germs can hardly form chains of infection any more
Because vaccinated people breathe out antibodies
Because unvaccinated people then have fewer contacts
121221.e: If almost everyone is immune, a germ rarely meets susceptible people. In this way babies or people with weak immune systems are protected indirectly; this is called herd protection.
121221.m: High vaccination coverage also protects unvaccinated people indirectly.

121222.q: Why can measles outbreaks happen despite a high national vaccination coverage rate?
a: Unvaccinated people are often clustered in certain groups or regions
The measles vaccine only protects for one year
Measles is only spread by vaccinated people
Measles viruses only survive in cities
121222.e: Averages hide local gaps in vaccination. Where unvaccinated people cluster, for example in certain communities, the virus can spread.
121222.m: Local vaccination gaps allow outbreaks despite good averages.

121223.q: In a municipality, 85 % of children are vaccinated, and the vaccine works in 95 % of those vaccinated. What share of the children is protected as a result?
121223.e: Protected are 0.85 times 0.95, which is 0.8075. That is around 81 % of all children.
121223.m: Only the share of vaccinated people with an effective immune response is protected.

121224.q: What does the vaccination record show when vaccination coverage is surveyed?
a: Which vaccinations are documented and with how many doses
How high the current antibody level is
Which diseases the child has already had
What blood group the child has
121224.e: The surveys analyse the entries in the vaccination record. They count the documented vaccinations and doses, not measured antibodies.
121224.m: Vaccination coverage rates are based on documented vaccinations.

121225.q: From what age does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend the yearly flu vaccination to everyone as a risk group?
121225.e: Older people have a much higher risk of severe flu and complications. That is why the flu vaccination is recommended to them every autumn.
121225.m: From 65, the flu vaccination is recommended every year.

121226.q: In the Swiss vaccination schedule, what are the vaccinations called that are recommended for everyone to protect personal and public health?
121226.e: The schedule distinguishes between basic vaccinations, supplementary vaccinations and vaccinations for risk groups. Basic vaccinations are recommended for the whole population, for example against measles or tetanus.
121226.m: Basic vaccinations are recommended for everyone.

121227.q: Against which three diseases does the MMR vaccination protect, which the Swiss vaccination schedule recommends for young children?
121227.e: MMR stands for measles, mumps and rubella. The schedule recommends two doses in early childhood so that reliable protection exists as early as possible.
121227.m: The MMR vaccination protects against measles, mumps and rubella.

121228.q: Apart from diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough, against which diseases does the six-in-one vaccination for babies protect?
a: Polio, Haemophilus influenzae type b and hepatitis B
121228.e: The hexavalent vaccine protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, Hib and hepatitis B. It is given several times in the first year of life.
121228.m: The six-in-one vaccination also covers polio, Hib and hepatitis B.

121229.q: Why does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend vaccinating babies in their first months of life?
a: Diseases such as whooping cough are especially dangerous for babies
Babies tolerate vaccinations better than adults
Later on vaccinations no longer work at all
Babies are protected against everything from birth
121229.e: Some infections, such as whooping cough, are particularly severe in babies and can be life-threatening. That is why protection should be built up as early as possible.
121229.m: Early vaccinations protect babies from dangerous diseases.

121230.q: At what age does the Swiss vaccination schedule recommend the hepatitis B vaccination if it was not given in infancy?
121230.e: The hepatitis B vaccination is preferably given in infancy. If it is missing, it should be caught up in young people between 11 and 15.
121230.m: Young people catch up on a missing hepatitis B vaccination at 11 to 15.

121231.q: Is there a general duty to be vaccinated in Switzerland?
a: No, vaccinations are voluntary in principle
Yes, but only in French-speaking Switzerland
Yes, for all children before kindergarten
121231.e: Vaccinations are voluntary in Switzerland. The law only allows the cantons, in exceptional cases, to make a vaccination compulsory for groups at risk or certain jobs.
121231.m: In Switzerland, vaccinations are voluntary in principle.

121232.q: In the Swiss vaccination schedule, what are vaccinations called that offer individual protection but are not counted as basic for everyone?
121232.e: Supplementary vaccinations mainly protect the vaccinated person against particular risks. Doctors give information about them, and the decision is an individual one.
121232.m: Supplementary vaccinations offer extra personal protection.

121233.q: What kind of body is the EKIF, the Federal Commission for Vaccination?
a: An extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation
A commission of the National Council
A private foundation of the pharmaceutical industry
121233.e: Extra-parliamentary commissions advise the Federal Council and the administration with outside expertise. The EKIF is such a commission for all questions about vaccinations.
121233.m: The EKIF is an extra-parliamentary commission of the Confederation.

121234.q: What is the main job of the EKIF?
a: It draws up vaccination recommendations and advises the FOPH and the Federal Council
It approves vaccines for the market
It produces vaccines for the army
It imposes fines for missing vaccinations
121234.e: The EKIF assesses scientific data and draws up vaccination recommendations together with the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH). Approving vaccines, by contrast, is the job of another federal authority.
121234.m: The EKIF draws up vaccination recommendations.

121235.q: Which authority, not the EKIF, is responsible for approving vaccines in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences
The Federal Office for the Environment
121235.e: Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness and grants approval. Only afterwards does the EKIF decide whether and for whom a vaccination is recommended.

121236.q: Who chooses the members of the EKIF?
121236.e: The EKIF is set up by the Federal Council. Its members are experts from medicine and healthcare.
121236.m: The Federal Council chooses the members of the EKIF.

121237.q: What is the German counterpart of the EKIF, based at the Robert Koch Institute, called?
121237.e: In Germany, STIKO publishes the vaccination recommendations. It has a similar role to the EKIF in Switzerland.

121238.q: What role do recommendations from the FOPH and the EKIF play in the cost of a vaccination in Switzerland?
a: Recommended vaccinations are usually paid for by basic health insurance
Recommended vaccinations always have to be paid for yourself
They have no influence on costs
121238.e: For many recommended vaccinations, compulsory health insurance covers the costs if they are listed in the health care benefits ordinance. Travel vaccinations are usually not covered.
121238.m: Recommended vaccinations are usually covered by basic health insurance.

121239.q: What kinds of data does the EKIF take into account for a new vaccination recommendation?
a: Burden of disease, effectiveness, safety and costs
Only the recommendations from the USA
121239.e: The commission weighs up how common and severe a disease is and how well and safely the vaccine works. Practicality and cost-effectiveness are also included.
121239.m: Vaccination recommendations are based on weighing up many data.

121240.q: Which organisation in the USA draws up vaccination recommendations in a similar way to the EKIF?
121240.e: ACIP advises the US health authority CDC on vaccination recommendations. The FDA approves vaccines, much like Swissmedic, and the NIH fund research.
121240.m: In the USA, ACIP recommends vaccinations and the FDA approves them.

121241.q: Roughly how high was the death rate for the severe form of smallpox, variola major?
121241.e: About one in three people who fell ill died of variola major. Many survivors were left with scars or went blind.
121241.m: The severe form of smallpox killed about one in three people who caught it.

121242.q: Who carried out the first vaccination with cowpox against smallpox in 1796?
121242.e: The English country doctor Edward Jenner vaccinated the boy James Phipps with material from cowpox. Afterwards the boy was protected against real smallpox.
121242.m: In 1796 Edward Jenner vaccinated with cowpox for the first time.

121243.q: Where does the word “vaccine” come from?
121243.e: The term recalls Jenner's vaccination with cowpox. “Vaccinia” was the name for cowpox.
121243.m: Vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.

121244.q: What was the older method called in which people were inoculated with material from real smallpox pustules?
121244.e: In variolation, material from smallpox patients was put into small cuts in the skin. This usually led to milder illness, but it was risky and could infect others.
121244.m: Variolation used real smallpox germs and was dangerous.

121245.q: In which year did the World Health Organization officially declare smallpox eradicated?
121245.e: After the last natural case in Somalia in 1977, the World Health Assembly confirmed the eradication on 8 May 1980. It was the first human disease to be eradicated.
121245.m: Smallpox has been considered eradicated since 1980.

121246.q: Which strategy was decisive in the smallpox eradication programme?
a: Surveillance and ring vaccination around every case
Building smallpox hospitals in every town
121246.e: Instead of vaccinating everyone, each case was tracked down and the contacts around it were vaccinated in a targeted way. This strategy is called “surveillance and containment”.
121246.m: Smallpox was eradicated with surveillance and ring vaccination.

121247.q: Which feature of smallpox made its eradication possible?
a: The virus had no animal reservoir
The virus was not very contagious
The virus only lived in mosquitoes
121247.e: Smallpox only infected humans, and sick people were easy to recognise by the pustules. In addition, there was a stable, effective vaccine with long protection.
121247.m: Without an animal reservoir, the smallpox virus could be eradicated.

121248.q: Which simple instrument made vaccinating against smallpox much easier from the late 1960s?
a: The glass syringe with a plunger
121248.e: The bifurcated needle held a drop of vaccine between its two prongs. It was cheap, saved vaccine and could be learned quickly even by non-specialists.
121248.m: The bifurcated needle helped with smallpox vaccination worldwide.

121249.q: Which other infectious disease was eradicated after smallpox, though it is an animal disease?
121249.e: Rinderpest was declared eradicated in 2011 by the World Organisation for Animal Health and the FAO. It is so far the only animal disease to have been eradicated.

121250.q: Which cells does the poliovirus damage in polio?
a: Motor nerve cells in the spinal cord
121250.e: The poliovirus can destroy the motor nerve cells in the front horn of the spinal cord. The muscles they supply then stop working, and floppy paralysis results.
121250.m: Polio destroys motor nerve cells in the spinal cord.

121251.q: How is the poliovirus mainly transmitted?
a: Faecal-oral, through dirty hands, water or food
121251.e: Polioviruses are enteroviruses and multiply in the gut. They are shed in the stool and passed on through contaminated water or hands.

121252.q: Roughly what share of infections with polioviruses lead to paralysis?
121252.e: The great majority of infections cause no symptoms or only mild ones. Fewer than one per cent lead to paralysis, which is why the virus can spread unnoticed.

121253.q: Who developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, approved in 1955?
121253.e: Jonas Salk inactivated the polioviruses with formaldehyde. His vaccine (IPV) is injected and is also used in Switzerland today.
121253.m: Jonas Salk developed the injected inactivated polio vaccine.

121254.q: What risk does Sabin's oral live polio vaccine carry?
a: Rarely, disease-causing vaccine viruses can develop from it
It often causes allergies to sugar
It does not protect against polio at all
It has to be repeated every year
121254.e: The weakened vaccine viruses are shed and can change in poorly vaccinated populations. In this way, circulating vaccine-derived polioviruses rarely arise.
121254.m: The oral polio vaccine can rarely give rise to disease-causing vaccine viruses.

121255.q: In which two countries was wild polio still endemic in 2025?
121255.e: Thanks to the global polio initiative, the wild virus has almost disappeared. As of 2025, it is only endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
121255.m: Wild polio is only endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan.

121256.q: Which types of wild poliovirus are already considered eradicated?
121256.e: Wild poliovirus type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015 and type 3 in 2019. Only type 1 is still circulating.
121256.m: Only wild poliovirus type 1 is still circulating.

121257.q: Which device kept polio patients with paralysed breathing muscles alive in the 1950s?
121257.e: The iron lung creates low pressure in a closed tank so that the chest rises. In this way patients could breathe despite paralysed breathing muscles.
121257.m: The iron lung helped polio patients breathe using low pressure.

121258.q: When was the WHO European Region certified polio-free?
121258.e: The WHO European Region, which includes Switzerland, was declared free of wild polio in June 2002. But the virus can still be brought in, so vaccination continues.
121258.m: Europe has been certified polio-free since 2002.

121259.q: What is the aim of contact tracing?
a: Finding contacts of infected people and breaking chains of infection
Developing new vaccines in the laboratory
Counting the number of hospital beds
121259.e: In contact tracing, people who have had contact with an infected person are identified. They are informed, tested or sent into quarantine before they infect others.
121259.m: Contact tracing breaks chains of infection.

121260.q: What is the difference between isolation and quarantine?
a: Isolation is for sick people, quarantine for people who may have been infected
Isolation is for animals, quarantine for humans
Isolation always lasts longer than a year
121260.e: People who are confirmed to be infected stay in isolation. Quarantine concerns healthy contacts who could have been infected and are therefore kept apart as a precaution.
121260.m: Isolation is for the sick, quarantine for those who may have been infected.

121261.q: What is it called when tracers find out where an infected person caught the infection themselves?
121261.e: Backward tracing looks for the source of infection, such as an event. In this way superspreading events and further cases from the same source are found.
121261.m: Backward tracing looks for the source of an infection.

121262.q: What is the first known infected person in an outbreak called?
121262.e: The index case is the starting point of the investigation. Contacts are traced from there.
121262.m: The index case stands at the start of contact tracing.

121263.q: Who was mainly responsible for contact tracing in Switzerland during the Covid-19 pandemic?
121263.e: Carrying out disease control is largely the job of the cantons. The cantonal medical services organised the contact tracing.
121263.m: In Switzerland, the cantons organise contact tracing.

121264.q: Which technology did the SwissCovid app use to record encounters?
121264.e: The app exchanged anonymous keys with nearby devices via Bluetooth. No locations were stored, and the matching took place in a decentralised way on the phone.
121264.m: The SwissCovid app used Bluetooth instead of location data.

121265.q: Which universities played a leading role in developing the decentralised DP-3T protocol for the SwissCovid app?
a: University of Basel and University of Bern
University of Geneva and University of Fribourg
121265.e: DP-3T stands for Decentralized Privacy-Preserving Proximity Tracing. It was developed by an international team led by EPFL and ETH Zurich.
121265.m: The DP-3T protocol comes from EPFL and ETH Zurich.

121266.q: Why does infection before symptoms start make contact tracing harder?
a: Infected people infect others before they know they are ill
Tests do not work at all before symptoms
121266.e: With presymptomatic transmission, tracing often starts too late. That is why testing and informing quickly are crucial.
121266.m: Presymptomatic transmission makes contact tracing harder.

121267.q: For how long are contacts usually monitored in the case of Ebola?
121267.e: The incubation period of Ebola is up to 21 days. Anyone who develops no symptoms during this time is considered not infected.
121267.m: With Ebola, contacts are watched for 21 days.

121567.q: Which feature do prokaryotes lack, unlike eukaryotes?
a: A nucleus with a nuclear envelope
121567.e: In prokaryotes, the DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm without being surrounded by a nuclear envelope. A cell membrane, ribosomes and cytoplasm, on the other hand, are found in all cells.

121568.q: Which two domains of life belong to the prokaryotes?
121568.e: In Carl Woese's three-domain system, bacteria and archaea are prokaryotic, and the eukaryotes form the third domain. Viruses are not considered living things with their own cells.
121568.m: Bacteria and archaea are the two groups of prokaryotes.

121569.q: What is the region in a bacterium's cytoplasm called where the ring-shaped chromosome lies?
121569.e: The nucleoid is a nuclear region without a membrane in which the bacterial chromosome is tightly packed. The nucleolus, by contrast, is part of the nucleus of eukaryotes.
121569.m: Bacterial DNA lies in the nucleoid without an envelope.

121570.q: Which type of ribosome do prokaryotes have?
121570.e: Prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes, while eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Many antibiotics use this difference and specifically block the 70S ribosomes.

121571.q: What substance is the cell wall of most bacteria mainly made of?
121571.e: Murein, also called peptidoglycan, is a network of sugar chains and short peptides. Cellulose is found in plant cell walls, chitin in fungi and insects.
121571.m: The bacterial cell wall is made of murein.

121572.q: What are the long, rotating structures that many bacteria use to move called?
121572.e: Bacterial flagella are turned like a propeller by a motor in the cell envelope. Cilia and pseudopodia, by contrast, are found in eukaryotic cells.

121573.q: What are the small, usually ring-shaped DNA molecules called that bacteria can have in addition to their chromosome?
121573.e: Plasmids copy themselves independently of the chromosome and often carry useful extra genes. Plastids, by contrast, are organelles of plant cells.
121573.m: Plasmids are small rings of DNA in bacteria.

121574.q: After which Danish doctor is the staining method named that divides bacteria into two groups by the structure of their cell wall?
121574.e: Hans Christian Gram developed the stain in 1884. Bacteria with a thick cell wall layer stain blue-violet, those with a thin layer and an outer membrane stain red.
121574.m: Gram staining distinguishes bacteria by their cell wall.

121575.q: What is the reproductive cycle of a phage called in which the host cell bursts after new phages have formed?
121575.e: In the lytic cycle, the bacterium immediately produces new phages until the cell is dissolved and releases them. Lysis means dissolving.
121575.m: In the lytic cycle, the bacterial cell is destroyed.

121576.q: What is the phage DNA called that is built into the bacterial chromosome in the lysogenic cycle?
121576.e: The prophage is copied along with every cell division without killing the bacterium. Only under stress can it be cut out and trigger the production of new phages.
121576.m: A built-in phage is called a prophage.

121577.q: What is the protein shell called that surrounds the genetic material of a phage?
121577.e: The capsid consists of many identical protein building blocks. In typical phages such as T4, it sits as a head on a tail with fibres.
121577.m: The capsid protects a virus's genetic material.

121578.q: What did Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase prove with bacteriophages in 1952?
a: That DNA is the genetic material
That proteins are the genetic material
That viruses have their own cells
121578.e: They labelled the DNA with radioactive phosphorus and the proteins with radioactive sulphur. Only the labelled DNA got into the bacteria.
121578.m: The Hershey-Chase experiment proved that DNA carries genetic information.

121579.q: What would people like to use bacteriophages for more often in medicine?
121579.e: Phages attack particular bacteria specifically, including those against which antibiotics no longer work. This phage therapy has a long tradition, especially in Georgia.
121579.m: Phages are a hope against resistant bacteria.

121580.q: Why are bacteriophages basically harmless to humans?
a: They do not survive in water
They are bigger than human cells
They are digested by the stomach at once
121580.e: Phages use their tail fibres to recognise very specific surface structures of bacteria. They cannot dock onto human cells.

121581.q: What does the Greek part “phage” in “bacteriophage” mean?
121581.e: Phagein means to eat or devour in Greek. A bacteriophage is therefore literally a bacteria eater.

121582.q: What is the transfer of bacterial genes from one cell to another with the help of phages called?
121582.e: In transduction, phages accidentally package pieces of bacterial DNA and carry them into the next bacterium. In transformation, by contrast, a bacterium takes up free DNA from its surroundings.
121582.m: In transduction, phages carry bacterial genes.

121583.q: What is the transfer of plasmids between two bacteria through direct cell contact via a pilus called?
121583.e: In conjugation, a donor bacterium forms a bridge to the recipient and transfers a copy of the plasmid. In this way resistance genes spread quickly, even between different species.
121583.m: Conjugation transfers plasmids through direct contact.

121584.q: Which enzyme makes many bacteria resistant to penicillins by splitting the active substance?
121584.e: Beta-lactamases destroy the penicillin molecule before it can work. That is why penicillins are often combined with inhibitors such as clavulanic acid.

121585.q: What is the approach called that looks at antibiotic resistance in humans, animals and the environment together?
121585.e: Resistant bacteria move back and forth between people, farm animals, food and water. That is why, in the One Health approach, human and veterinary medicine, farming and environmental protection work together.
121585.m: Resistance is best fought with the One Health approach.

121586.q: Which evolutionary process explains why resistant bacteria increase during antibiotic treatment?
121586.e: The antibiotic kills sensitive bacteria, while resistant ones survive and multiply. In this way resistance spreads through the bacterial population.

121587.q: What is meant by horizontal gene transfer in bacteria?
a: Genes are exchanged between existing cells
Genes are only passed on to daughter cells
121587.e: In horizontal gene transfer, genes pass not through division but sideways from one bacterium to another. This can even happen between different bacterial species.
121587.m: Horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance genes between bacteria.

121588.q: When is a germ described as multi-resistant?
a: When it is resistant to several classes of antibiotics
When disinfectants do not affect it
121588.e: Multi-resistant germs no longer respond to several groups of antibiotics. This makes treatment difficult and expensive.
121588.m: Multi-resistant germs defy several groups of antibiotics.

121589.q: What is the main aim of the Swiss Strategy on Antibiotic Resistance (StAR)?
a: To keep antibiotics effective in the long term
To sell antibiotics without a prescription
121589.e: The StAR strategy was adopted by the Federal Council in 2015. It includes measures in human and veterinary medicine and in farming so that antibiotics remain effective.
121589.m: Switzerland fights antibiotic resistance with the StAR strategy.

121590.q: Which behaviour by patients encourages antibiotic resistance to develop?
a: Stopping or changing the course without talking to the doctor
Telling the doctor about side effects
121590.e: Anyone who stops antibiotics on their own, takes the wrong dose or later takes leftover tablets themselves exposes bacteria to the drug unnecessarily or insufficiently. This helps resistant germs survive.
121590.m: Take antibiotics exactly as the doctor prescribes.

121591.q: Which aminopenicillin is very often prescribed today, for example for middle ear infections?
121591.e: Amoxicillin is a penicillin with a wider range of action that is well absorbed from the gut. Ciprofloxacin, doxycycline and clarithromycin belong to other classes of antibiotics.
121591.m: Amoxicillin is a commonly used penicillin.

121592.q: What did Alexander Fleming observe in 1928 that led to the discovery of penicillin?
a: A mould stopped bacteria growing in a culture dish
121592.e: Fleming noticed that no bacteria grew around a mould of the genus Penicillium. The mould produced a substance that he called penicillin.

121593.q: Why was penicillin only used as a medicine more than ten years after its discovery?
a: It was difficult to make it pure and in large amounts
It was banned at the time
At first it only worked on plants
Nobody had recognised bacteria as germs
121593.e: Only around 1940 did Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in Oxford manage to purify penicillin and show its healing effect. For this they received the Nobel Prize with Fleming in 1945.
121593.m: Florey and Chain turned penicillin into a medicine.

121594.q: How does penicillin act on bacteria?
a: It blocks the building of the cell wall
It dissolves the cell membrane at once
121594.e: Penicillin blocks enzymes that cross-link the network of sugar chains and peptides in the cell wall. Growing bacteria therefore become unstable and burst.
121594.m: Penicillin disrupts the building of the bacterial cell wall.

121595.q: Which ring structure in the molecule is crucial for penicillin's effect?
121595.e: The strained four-membered beta-lactam ring binds to the enzymes that build the cell wall and blocks them. Cephalosporins also have this ring.
121595.m: Penicillins belong to the beta-lactam antibiotics.

121596.q: Against which bacteria does penicillin G mainly work?
121596.e: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick cell wall layer that is easy to reach. In gram-negative bacteria, an outer membrane protects the thin cell wall layer.
121596.m: Penicillin G works especially well against gram-positive germs.

121597.q: Why is penicillin G usually injected rather than swallowed?
a: It is destroyed by stomach acid
It does not dissolve in water
It is stored straight away by the liver
121597.e: Penicillin G is sensitive to acid and would be largely broken down in the stomach. Penicillin V is more stable in acid and can be taken as a tablet.

121598.q: Which unwanted reaction to penicillin is the best known?
121598.e: Penicillin allergies are among the most common drug allergies and range from skin rashes to anaphylactic shock. Discoloured teeth, by contrast, are typical of tetracyclines.

121599.q: What do staphylococci typically look like under the microscope?
a: Spheres in clusters like bunches of grapes
121599.e: Staphylé is the Greek word for a bunch of grapes. Spherical bacteria in chains, by contrast, are streptococci.
121599.m: Staphylococci lie together like bunches of grapes.

121600.q: Where does Staphylococcus aureus live in many healthy people without making them ill?
121600.e: Around 20 to 30 per cent of people carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nose, some of them permanently. It only becomes dangerous when it gets into the body, for example through wounds.
121600.m: Many healthy people carry staphylococci in their nose.

121601.q: Which measure is most important in hospital to prevent MRSA from being passed on?
a: Taking the temperature of all visitors
121601.e: MRSA is mainly carried from patient to patient on the hands of staff. Hand disinfection breaks this route most effectively.
121601.m: Hand disinfection stops MRSA from spreading.

121602.q: What does the “R” in the abbreviation MRSA stand for?
