a: Hair root cells divide quickly and are damaged too
The medicines dissolve the hair chemically
The scalp is cooled during the treatment
The body needs the hair as an energy reserve
123244.e: Cytostatic drugs hit all cells that divide rapidly. Besides cancer cells, these include the cells of the hair roots. After treatment the hair usually grows back.
123244.m: Hair loss happens because hair root cells also divide quickly.

123245.q: From which chemical warfare agent were the first cytostatic drugs developed in the 1940s?
123245.e: It was observed that mustard gas greatly reduces the number of white blood cells. This led to the nitrogen mustard compounds that were used against lymphomas.
123245.m: The first chemotherapy drugs go back to mustard gas.

123246.q: What distinguishes a targeted cancer therapy such as imatinib, developed in Basel, from classic chemotherapy?
a: It specifically blocks a particular cancer protein
It is always used during surgery
It irradiates the tumour from outside
123246.e: Classic cytostatic drugs damage all cells that divide quickly. Imatinib, by contrast, specifically inhibits an overactive enzyme in leukaemia cells and so tends to spare healthy cells.
123246.m: Targeted cancer therapies attack a particular cancer protein.

123247.q: Why is chemotherapy sometimes given before a cancer operation?
a: To make the wound heal faster
123247.e: A smaller tumour can be removed more easily and more completely. Specialists call treatment before an operation neoadjuvant.
123247.m: Chemotherapy before an operation can shrink the tumour.

123248.q: What do many cytostatic drugs disrupt in cancer cells so that they can no longer divide?
123248.e: Before each division, a cell must copy its DNA. Many cytostatic drugs block this step, for example by depriving the cell of DNA building blocks.
123248.m: Cytostatic drugs prevent DNA copying before cell division.

123249.q: Why is chemotherapy usually given in cycles with breaks?
a: So that healthy tissue can recover
So that the tumour grows faster
Because otherwise the medicines go off
Because hospitals are closed at night
123249.e: Healthy dividing cells, for example in the bone marrow, are also damaged. During the breaks they can regenerate before the next cycle.
123249.m: Breaks between cycles protect healthy tissue.

123250.q: Which glial cells form an important part of the blood-brain barrier with their extensions?
123250.e: Astrocytes wrap their end feet around the blood capillaries in the brain. Together with the tightly connected vessel cells, they control which substances get into the brain.
123250.m: Astrocytes are important for the blood-brain barrier.

123251.q: At which point on a nerve cell is it decided whether an action potential is triggered?
123251.e: At the axon hillock, the incoming signals are added up. If the threshold is exceeded there, an action potential arises and travels along the axon.
123251.m: The axon hillock decides whether an action potential is triggered.

123252.q: What is the point of contact between a motor nerve fibre and a skeletal muscle fibre called?
123252.e: At the motor end plate, the nerve ending passes the impulse on to the muscle fibre. This special synapse triggers every voluntary movement.
123252.m: At the motor end plate, the nerve controls the muscle.

123253.q: Which neurotransmitter is released when a motor nerve stimulates a skeletal muscle?
123253.e: Acetylcholine binds to receptors in the muscle fibre membrane and opens ion channels. The arrow poison curare blocks these receptors and so paralyses the muscles.
123253.m: Acetylcholine transmits the signal from the nerve to the skeletal muscle.

123401.q: Which plants are typical of the Arctic tundra?
123401.e: Only low plants that can cope with cold and a short growing season grow in the tundra. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly reach knee height.
123401.m: The tundra is dominated by mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.

123542.q: Why can you not see the DNA double helix in a light microscope?
a: It is only a few nanometres thick
It is as transparent as water
123542.e: The double helix is only around 2 nanometres thick. Light microscopes only show structures from about 200 nanometres.
123542.m: The DNA double helix is too thin for the light microscope.

123543.q: Whose X-ray diffraction image (Photo 51) provided an important clue to the helical structure of DNA?
123543.e: Rosalind Franklin and her doctoral student Raymond Gosling took the famous image “Photo 51”. The typical X-shaped pattern points to a helix.
123543.m: Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 revealed the helical shape of DNA.

123544.q: What is the “backbone” of every DNA strand made of?
123544.e: The nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds between the sugar deoxyribose and phosphate groups. The bases point inwards.
123544.m: Sugar and phosphate form the backbone of DNA.

123545.q: Roughly how many base pairs make up one turn of the common B-DNA?
123545.e: In the B form of DNA, one full turn of the helix contains around 10 to 10.5 base pairs. This can be worked out from X-ray diffraction data.
123545.m: One turn of B-DNA has around ten base pairs.

123546.q: Roughly what diameter does the DNA double helix have?
123546.e: B-DNA is about 2 nanometres thick. That makes it far too thin to be visible in a light microscope.
123546.m: The DNA double helix is only around two nanometres thick.

123547.q: In which direction is natural B-DNA twisted?
123547.e: B-DNA is a right-handed helix. There is also left-handed Z-DNA, but it is rare.
123547.m: Normal DNA is a right-handed helix.

123548.q: Which bonds hold the two strands of the double helix together?
123548.e: The opposite bases are connected by hydrogen bonds. In addition, stacking forces between the bases stabilise the helix.
123548.m: Hydrogen bonds connect the two DNA strands.

123549.q: What are the two grooves of different widths on the surface of the double helix called?
123549.e: Because the sugars of the two strands do not lie exactly opposite each other, a major and a minor groove form. Many proteins bind to the DNA there.
123549.m: The double helix has a major and a minor groove.

123550.q: What is the complementary strand to 5'-ATGC-3', also written from 5' to 3'?
123550.e: The complement of ATGC is TACG, but it runs from 3' to 5'. Read in the 5' to 3' direction, this gives GCAT.
123550.m: The complementary strand is written as the complement and reversed.

123551.q: What pairs with the codon of the mRNA during translation?
a: The start codon of the DNA
123551.e: Each tRNA carries an anticodon of three bases. It pairs complementarily with the matching codon of the mRNA and so brings the correct amino acid to the ribosome.
123551.m: The anticodon of the tRNA recognises the codon of the mRNA.

123552.q: What happens to the base pairs when DNA is heated to over 90 degrees Celsius?
a: They come apart and the strands separate
123552.e: When heated, the bonds between the opposite bases break and the DNA denatures. This melting is used in PCR.
123552.m: Heat separates the two DNA strands.

123553.q: How many hydrogen bonds connect an adenine-thymine pair?
123553.e: Adenine and thymine are connected by two hydrogen bonds. Sections rich in AT can therefore be separated more easily.
123553.m: An AT pair is held together by two hydrogen bonds.

123554.e: Purines have a double-ring system; they include adenine and guanine. Cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines with only one ring.
123554.m: Adenine and guanine are purines with two rings.

123555.q: Why does every base pair consist of one purine and one pyrimidine?
a: So that the helix is the same width everywhere
So that the DNA becomes water-soluble
So that enzymes can break it down faster
So that the strands never separate
123555.e: A large purine and a small pyrimidine together always give roughly the same length. In this way the distance between the two backbones stays constant.
123555.m: Purine plus pyrimidine keeps the helix the same width.

123556.q: Which base replaces thymine in RNA?
123556.e: In RNA, the base uracil is found instead of thymine. Uracil also pairs with adenine.
123556.m: In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine.

123557.q: What does Chargaff's rule state for double-stranded DNA?
a: Adenine and thymine occur equally often
All four bases occur equally often
Purines are twice as common as pyrimidines
Guanine is always the most common base
123557.e: Erwin Chargaff found that the proportion of adenine equals that of thymine, and that of guanine equals that of cytosine. This fits with complementary base pairing.
123557.m: According to Chargaff, there is as much adenine as thymine.

123558.q: A double-stranded DNA contains 20 per cent adenine. What is the proportion of guanine?
123558.e: Thymine also makes up 20 per cent, so together 40 per cent. The remaining 60 per cent are shared equally between guanine and cytosine, so 30 per cent each.
123558.m: The proportion of guanine can be calculated from the proportion of adenine.

123559.q: What is the type of DNA copying called in which each new double helix keeps one old strand?
123559.e: In semi-conservative replication, each parent strand serves as a template. Each daughter DNA consists of one old and one new strand.

123560.q: Which researchers proved semi-conservative replication with heavy nitrogen in 1958?
123560.e: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl labelled bacterial DNA with the isotope 15N. The density of the DNA after each division showed the semi-conservative pattern.
123560.m: Meselson and Stahl proved semi-conservative copying.

123561.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA at the replication fork?
123561.e: Helicase separates the two strands by pulling the base pairs apart. For this it needs energy from ATP.

123562.q: In which direction does DNA polymerase extend a new strand?
123562.e: DNA polymerase only adds new nucleotides to the 3' end. The new strand therefore grows from 5' to 3'.
123562.m: DNA polymerases always build from 5' to 3'.

123563.q: Which enzyme makes the short RNA starter pieces for DNA polymerase?
123563.e: DNA polymerase cannot start on its own; it needs a free 3' end. Primase supplies an RNA primer for this.
123563.m: Primase lays down the starting primer.

123564.q: Which enzyme joins the Okazaki fragments into a continuous strand?
123564.e: DNA ligase closes the last gaps in the sugar-phosphate backbone. This produces a strand without gaps.
123564.m: Ligase sticks pieces of DNA together.

123565.q: Which property of many DNA polymerases lowers the error rate during replication?
123565.e: Many DNA polymerases recognise wrongly inserted nucleotides and remove them with their exonuclease activity. This checking is called proofreading.

123566.q: Which enzyme prevents the DNA ahead of the replication fork from becoming too tightly twisted?
123566.e: Unwinding creates tension ahead of the fork. Topoisomerases briefly cut the DNA and so release the overwinding.

123567.q: Where does transcription take place in cells with a nucleus?
123567.e: In eukaryotes the DNA lies in the nucleus, so it is copied there. The finished mRNA is then exported into the cytoplasm.
123567.m: In eukaryotes, transcription takes place in the nucleus.

123568.q: What is the DNA region called where RNA polymerase begins transcription?
123568.e: The promoter is a recognition sequence in front of the gene. Transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind there.

123569.q: Which well-known sequence is found in many eukaryotic promoters?
123569.e: The TATA box lies just before the starting point of many genes. It serves as a binding site for transcription factors.
123569.m: Many promoters contain a TATA box.

123570.q: What is the DNA strand called that is read as a template during transcription?
123570.e: The template strand is read. The RNA produced therefore has the sequence of the other, coding strand, only made of RNA building blocks.
123570.m: RNA polymerase reads the template strand.

123571.q: What is removed from the pre-mRNA during splicing?
123571.e: Introns are non-coding sections and are cut out. The exons are joined to form the mature mRNA.

123572.q: Which two modifications does eukaryotic mRNA receive at its ends?
123572.e: A cap of modified guanine is added to the 5' end, and a tail of many adenine nucleotides to the 3' end. Both protect the mRNA from being broken down.
123572.m: The cap and poly-A tail protect the mRNA.

123573.q: What does alternative splicing make possible?
123573.e: Depending on which exons are joined, different mature mRNAs are produced. In this way one gene can code for several versions of a protein.
123573.m: Alternative splicing makes several proteins from one gene.

123574.q: What guides a ribosome with its growing protein chain to the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
a: A signal peptide at the start of the chain
A stop codon at the end of the mRNA
The poly-A tail of the mRNA
123574.e: Proteins for membranes or for export carry a signal sequence at the start. It is recognised and the ribosome docks onto the rough ER.
123574.m: A signal peptide sends ribosomes to the rough ER.

123575.q: How large are eukaryotic ribosomes, given as a sedimentation coefficient?
123575.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, bacterial ones only 70S. The difference matters for some antibiotics.

123576.q: What is the group of three on the tRNA called that attaches to the codon of the mRNA?
123576.e: The anticodon is complementary to the codon. This ensures that the correct amino acid is built in.
123576.m: The anticodon of the tRNA recognises the codon.

123577.q: Which bond links the amino acids during translation?
123577.e: The ribosome links the carboxyl group of one amino acid to the amino group of the next. In the process, water is released.

123578.q: What are the three tRNA binding sites in the ribosome called?
123578.e: The loaded tRNA arrives at the A site, the growing chain hangs at the P site, and the empty tRNA leaves the ribosome via the E site.
123578.m: The ribosome has an A, a P and an E site.

123579.q: Which enzyme loads each tRNA with the matching amino acid?
123579.e: There is a separate aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase for each amino acid. Using ATP, it links the amino acid to the correct tRNA.
123579.m: Synthetases load tRNAs with amino acids.

123580.q: What binds to the ribosome when a stop codon is reached?
123580.e: There is no matching tRNA for stop codons. A release factor binds and releases the finished chain.

123581.q: What is an mRNA called that is read by several ribosomes at the same time?
123581.e: Several ribosomes can work one behind the other on the same mRNA. In this way many copies of a protein are made in a short time.
123581.m: A polysome is many ribosomes on one mRNA.

123582.q: What is different in bacteria compared with eukaryotes as regards transcription and translation?
a: They can take place at the same time
They only take place at night
123582.e: Bacteria have no nucleus. Ribosomes can therefore attach to the mRNA while it is still being transcribed.
123582.m: In bacteria, transcription and translation are coupled.

123583.q: Which amino acid is coded by the start codon AUG?
123583.e: AUG marks the start of translation and at the same time codes for methionine. That is why newly made proteins initially begin with methionine.
123583.m: The start codon AUG stands for methionine.

123585.q: How many stop codons does the standard code contain?
123585.e: The stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. There is no matching tRNA for them.
123585.m: The standard code has three stop codons.

123586.q: Which codon is the usual start codon?
123586.e: The codon AUG marks the start of translation. At the same time it codes for methionine.

123587.q: For how many standard amino acids does the genetic code code?
123587.e: The sense codons are distributed among 20 canonical amino acids. In addition there are the stop codons.
123587.m: The genetic code specifies 20 amino acids.

123588.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is “degenerate”?
a: Several codons stand for the same amino acid
One codon stands for several amino acids
123588.e: Because there are more codons than amino acids, most amino acids are coded more than once. This is also called redundancy.
123588.m: Many amino acids are coded by several codons.

123589.q: What does it mean that the genetic code is almost universal?
a: Almost all living things use the same code
Every gene has the same code
The code is the same length in all proteins
123589.e: Bacteria, plants and humans translate codons almost identically. That is why a human gene can be read in bacteria; there are small differences, for example in mitochondria.
123589.m: Almost all living things use the same genetic code.

123590.q: Which circular table is used in biology lessons to read off which amino acid a codon codes for?
123590.e: In the codon wheel, a codon is read from the inside out. On the outside you find the matching amino acid or the stop signal.
123590.m: The codon wheel translates codons into amino acids.

123591.q: What is a mutation called in which a single base is exchanged for another?
123591.e: In a substitution, one base is replaced and the length of the DNA stays the same. It is a form of point mutation.
123591.m: In a substitution, one base is exchanged.

123592.q: What does the deletion of a single base in a gene usually cause?
a: A shift in the reading frame
123592.e: Because the codons are read in groups of three, all the following triplets shift. This usually produces a completely changed or shortened protein.
123592.m: If a base is missing, the reading frame shifts.

123593.q: What is a mutation called that does not change the amino acid sequence?
123593.e: Because of multiple coding, a new codon can stand for the same amino acid. The protein then stays the same.
123593.m: A silent mutation does not change the protein.

123594.q: What is created in a nonsense mutation?
123594.e: If a codon becomes a stop codon, translation breaks off too early. The protein is shortened and usually does not work.
123594.m: A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.

123595.q: What is a point mutation called that leads to a different amino acid being built in?
123595.e: In a missense mutation, the changed codon codes for a different amino acid. The consequences range from harmless to severe.
123595.m: A missense mutation exchanges one amino acid.

123596.q: Which DNA damage does UV radiation typically cause?
123596.e: UV light links two neighbouring thymines together. If these dimers are not repaired, mutations and skin cancer can result.
123596.m: UV radiation creates thymine dimers in DNA.

123597.q: Which type of mutation is trisomy 21?
123597.e: In a genome mutation, the number of chromosomes is changed. In trisomy 21, chromosome 21 is present three times.
123597.m: In trisomy 21, the number of chromosomes is changed.

123598.q: What are substances or radiation that trigger mutations called?
123598.e: Mutagens increase the mutation rate. Examples are ionising radiation, UV light and certain chemicals in tobacco smoke.

123599.q: What are sections of DNA called that can change their position in the genome?
123599.e: Transposons are also called jumping genes. They make up a large part of the human genome.
123599.m: Transposons can jump around in the genome.

123600.q: Roughly what percentage of the genome do two people share?
123600.e: Two people differ in only about one in every thousand building blocks. Even so, these small differences account for a great deal of variety.

123601.q: What share of the human genome codes directly for proteins?
123601.e: Only a small part of the DNA consists of exons, which code for proteins. The rest includes introns, regulatory sections and repeats.
123601.m: Only a small part of the genome codes for proteins.

123602.q: Roughly how long would all the DNA in a human body cell be if stretched out?
123602.e: A diploid cell contains around 6 billion base pairs, which stretched out gives about 2 metres. The DNA is wound around histones and highly compacted.
123602.m: The DNA of one cell is around two metres long when stretched out.

123603.q: Which cell organelles have their own small genome?
123603.e: Mitochondria have a ring-shaped DNA with a few genes. This is seen as evidence that they originated from bacteria.

123604.q: What shape is the main chromosome of most bacteria?
123604.e: Most bacteria have a closed, ring-shaped chromosome. In addition, small plasmids may be present.
123604.m: Bacteria usually have a ring-shaped chromosome.

123605.q: Some amoebae and lungfish have much more DNA than humans. What does this show?
a: Genome size and complexity are hardly related
These animals are more complex than humans
123605.e: The amount of DNA says little about how complex a living thing is. A large part of many genomes consists of repeats and non-coding sections.
123605.m: A large genome does not mean a complex living thing.

123606.q: What is the field called that studies whole genomes?
123606.e: Genomics studies the structure, function and comparison of complete genomes. Proteomics, by contrast, studies the whole set of proteins.

123607.q: In which year did the public Human Genome Project officially start?
123607.e: The project was launched in 1990, mainly by US authorities. Research centres from several countries soon took part.
123607.m: The Human Genome Project began in 1990.

123608.q: Which researcher competed with the public project with the company Celera Genomics?
123608.e: With Celera, Craig Venter relied on fast shotgun sequencing. The race sped up the whole undertaking.
123608.m: Craig Venter challenged the public project with Celera.

123609.q: Which sequencing method was mainly used in the Human Genome Project?
123609.e: Frederick Sanger's chain termination method was highly automated. Modern high-throughput methods only came later.
123609.m: The human genome was sequenced with the Sanger method.

123610.q: In which year were the first draft versions of the human genome published in scientific journals?
123610.e: The draft was publicly announced in 2000, and the publications appeared in “Nature” and “Science” in 2001.
123610.m: The draft sequence of the human genome appeared in 2001.

123611.q: Who led the public Human Genome Project in its main phase?
123611.e: James Watson led the US part at the beginning; from 1993 Francis Collins took over. Collins led the project until it was completed.
123611.m: Francis Collins led the Human Genome Project to its goal.

123612.q: Roughly how much did the Human Genome Project cost?
123612.e: The public project cost around 3 billion US dollars. Today sequencing a genome costs only a tiny fraction of that.
123612.m: The Human Genome Project cost around three billion dollars.

123613.q: What did researchers achieve with the human genome in 2022?
a: The first complete sequence without gaps
The discovery of the DNA double helix
123613.e: The 2003 sequence still had gaps, for example at the centromeres. In 2022 they were closed with new long-read methods.
123613.m: Only in 2022 was a human genome sequenced without gaps.

123614.q: Which substance did the Swiss scientist Friedrich Miescher discover in 1869?
123614.e: Miescher isolated a new substance from cell nuclei and called it nuclein. Today we know that it was mainly DNA.
123614.m: Friedrich Miescher discovered nucleic acid in 1869.

123615.q: In which city was Friedrich Miescher born?
123615.e: Friedrich Miescher was born in Basel in 1844. He came from a Basel family of doctors.

123616.q: From what material did Miescher obtain his first cell nuclei?
123616.e: He used white blood cells from the pus on used dressings from a hospital. These cells have large nuclei.
123616.m: Miescher found nuclein in white blood cells from pus.

123617.q: In which city did Miescher make his discovery?
123617.e: Miescher worked in Felix Hoppe-Seyler's laboratory at Hohentübingen Castle. There he isolated nuclein.

123618.q: Which element was strikingly abundant in nuclein and distinguished it from proteins?
123618.e: Miescher's analyses showed a high phosphorus content. This made it clear that it was not an ordinary protein.

123619.q: At which university was Miescher later professor of physiology?
123619.e: In 1872 Miescher became professor of physiology at the University of Basel. There he continued to study nuclein, among other things in salmon sperm.
123619.m: Miescher later taught at the University of Basel.

123620.q: From what did Miescher later obtain large amounts of nuclein in Basel?
123620.e: Salmon from the Rhine provided Miescher with sperm cells with very large nuclei. From these he could obtain and study a lot of nuclein.
123620.m: In Basel, Miescher studied nuclein from salmon sperm.

123621.q: In which place in the Grisons did Friedrich Miescher die in 1895?
123621.e: Miescher had tuberculosis and sought a cure in Davos. He died there in 1895.

123622.q: Which protein is often used as “gene scissors” in the CRISPR method?
123622.e: Cas9 is an endonuclease that cuts DNA at a chosen point. That is why people speak of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors.
123622.m: Cas9 is the best-known pair of gene scissors.

123623.q: Which two researchers received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for CRISPR/Cas9?
123623.e: In 2012 Charpentier and Doudna showed that Cas9 can be programmed precisely. For this they were honoured in 2020.
123623.m: Charpentier and Doudna received the Nobel Prize for CRISPR.

123624.q: What is the CRISPR system originally used for in bacteria?
123624.e: Bacteria store pieces of virus DNA in their CRISPR section. In a new infection, Cas recognises and cuts up the virus DNA.
123624.m: CRISPR is originally an immune system of bacteria.

123625.q: What steers Cas9 to the right place on the DNA?
123625.e: The guide RNA is complementary to the target sequence. It leads Cas9 exactly there.
123625.m: A guide RNA shows Cas9 where to cut.

123626.q: What does the enzyme Cas9 do to the DNA in the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors?
a: It cuts both DNA strands at a particular point
It translates the DNA into a protein
123626.e: Cas9 is an enzyme that cuts through DNA at a precisely chosen point. The cell then repairs the cut, and in the process the gene can be changed.
123626.m: Cas9 is the blade of the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors.

123627.q: What can be achieved with the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors by cutting a gene at a chosen point?
123627.e: The cell often repairs the cut inaccurately. This produces small errors that frequently switch the gene off.
123627.m: A targeted cut with CRISPR can switch a gene off.

123628.q: What is CRISPR/Cas9 mainly used for in research today?
a: To change genes in a targeted way
To stain viruses under the microscope
123628.e: CRISPR/Cas9 is also called gene scissors. It can be used to cut and change genes at precisely chosen points.
123628.m: CRISPR/Cas9 is a pair of gene scissors for changing genes precisely.

123629.q: For which hereditary disease was the first CRISPR therapy approved in 2023?
123629.e: The therapy Casgevy was approved in 2023, first in Great Britain and the USA. It is also used to treat beta thalassaemia.
123629.m: The first approved CRISPR therapy treats a blood disease.

123630.e: Only someone who carries two changed alleles has the disease. People with one changed allele are healthy.

123631.q: Which organ is particularly affected in cystic fibrosis?
123631.e: In cystic fibrosis the body produces sticky mucus. It mainly blocks the airways and leads to frequent chest infections; digestive organs are also affected.
123631.m: Cystic fibrosis makes the mucus in the lungs sticky.

123632.e: A single changed allele is enough for the disease. It usually only appears in adulthood.

123633.q: Which organ is progressively damaged in Huntington's disease?
123633.e: In Huntington's disease, nerve cells in the brain gradually die. This leads to involuntary movements and to changes in thinking and behaviour.
123633.m: Huntington's disease is a hereditary disease of the brain.

123634.q: What advantage do healthy carriers of a sickle cell allele have in some regions?
a: They are better protected against malaria
123634.e: Heterozygous carriers fall seriously ill with malaria less often. That is why the allele is common in malaria regions.
123634.m: The sickle cell allele partly protects carriers against malaria.

a: With a diet low in phenylalanine
123635.e: In phenylketonuria, the body cannot break down phenylalanine. A special low-protein diet started early prevents brain damage; newborns in Switzerland are tested for it.
123635.m: A diet low in phenylalanine helps with phenylketonuria.

123636.q: Both parents are healthy carriers of the same recessive disease allele. What is the risk that a child will have the disease?
123636.e: Each parent passes on the changed allele with a probability of 50 per cent. Together this gives 0.5 times 0.5, so 25 per cent.
123636.m: Two carriers have a one-in-four risk for each child.

123637.q: What is a person called who carries a recessive disease allele but is healthy?
123637.e: A carrier is heterozygous and shows no symptoms. However, they can pass the allele on.
123637.m: Healthy people with a recessive disease allele are called carriers.

123931.q: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
123931.e: The enzymes of glycolysis are dissolved in the cytoplasm. That is why it can also take place in cells without mitochondria.
123931.m: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.

123932.q: Which end product is formed from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
123932.e: Glucose, with six carbon atoms, is split into two C3 units and oxidised to two pyruvate molecules.
123932.m: Glycolysis makes two pyruvate from one glucose.

123933.q: How many ATP does the cell gain net from one molecule of glucose in glycolysis?
123933.e: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP at the start and later forms 4 ATP. That leaves a net 2 ATP per glucose.
123933.m: Glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose.

123934.q: What is the main purpose of converting pyruvate into lactate when oxygen is lacking?
a: It produces a lot of extra ATP
123934.e: Glycolysis needs NAD+ as an electron acceptor. Without oxygen, it is only made available again through the formation of lactate.
123934.m: Lactate formation keeps glycolysis going by recovering NAD+.

a: No, it also works without oxygen
Yes, it always needs a lot of oxygen
Yes, but only in the nucleus
123935.e: Glycolysis is anaerobic. That is why yeasts during fermentation or muscles short of oxygen can also gain energy from it.

123936.q: What happens to the pyruvate from glycolysis when there is enough oxygen?
a: It is broken down further in the mitochondria
It is stored in the nucleus
123936.e: With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondria. There it is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water via the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain.
123936.m: With oxygen, pyruvate is broken down further in the mitochondria.

123937.q: Why do red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis for their energy?
a: They have no contact with glucose
They do not need to transport oxygen
123937.e: Mature erythrocytes have neither a nucleus nor mitochondria. They therefore lack the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain.
123937.m: Red blood cells only gain ATP through glycolysis.

123938.q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place in human cells?
123938.e: The enzymes of the citric acid cycle are in the matrix of the mitochondria. Only succinate dehydrogenase sits in the inner membrane.
123938.m: The citric acid cycle takes place in the matrix of the mitochondria.

123939.q: With which molecule does acetyl-CoA react at the start of the citric acid cycle to form citrate?
123939.e: Citrate synthase links the C2 unit from acetyl-CoA with the C4 molecule oxaloacetate to form citrate with six carbon atoms.
123939.m: Acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate together form citrate.

123940.q: After which biochemist is the citric acid cycle also named?
123940.e: Hans Adolf Krebs described the cycle in the 1930s. That is why it is also called the Krebs cycle.
123940.m: After Hans Krebs, the citric acid cycle is also called the Krebs cycle.

123941.q: How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released per turn of the citric acid cycle?
123941.e: In two oxidative decarboxylations, one CO2 is split off each time. This corresponds to the two carbon atoms from the acetyl-CoA fed in.
123941.m: Each turn of the citric acid cycle releases two carbon dioxide.

123942.q: Which reducing equivalents does one turn of the citric acid cycle supply?
123942.e: Three dehydrogenases transfer hydrogen to NAD+, and succinate dehydrogenase to FAD. The electrons then go into the respiratory chain.
123942.m: One turn of the citric acid cycle supplies three NADH and one FADH2.

123943.q: What are the substances NADH and FADH2 formed in the citric acid cycle used for?
a: They supply electrons for the respiratory chain
123943.e: NADH and FADH2 hand their electrons over to the respiratory chain. There most of the ATP is gained from them.
123943.m: NADH and FADH2 bring electrons to the respiratory chain.

123944.q: Which enzyme complex links glycolysis with the citric acid cycle?
123944.e: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, splitting off CO2. This step cannot be reversed.
123944.m: Pyruvate dehydrogenase turns pyruvate into acetyl-CoA.

123945.q: Why does the citric acid cycle quickly come to a standstill without oxygen, even though it does not use oxygen itself?
a: NAD+ and FAD are no longer regenerated
Citrate breaks down immediately without oxygen
123945.e: The respiratory chain only oxidises NADH and FADH2 with oxygen as the final acceptor. Without it, the cycle runs out of oxidised coenzymes.
123945.m: The citric acid cycle needs oxygen indirectly, because the respiratory chain recovers its coenzymes.

123946.q: In which structure are the complexes of the respiratory chain located?
123946.e: The enzyme complexes are built into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Its folds, the cristae, increase the surface area.
123946.m: The respiratory chain lies in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

123947.q: Which substance is the final electron acceptor of the respiratory chain?
123947.e: At complex IV the electrons are transferred to oxygen. Together with protons, this produces water.
123947.m: Oxygen takes up the electrons at the end of the respiratory chain.

123948.q: Which enzyme uses the backflow of protons into the mitochondrial matrix to make ATP?
123948.e: ATP synthase works like a tiny turbine. When protons flow back through it, it turns and joins ADP and phosphate to form ATP.
123948.m: ATP synthase makes ATP using the proton gradient.

123949.q: What do complexes I, III and IV of the respiratory chain pump across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
123949.e: The energy from electron transfer is used to pump protons into the intermembrane space. This creates an electrochemical gradient.
123949.m: The respiratory chain pumps protons out of the matrix.

123950.q: Which complex of the respiratory chain does the poison cyanide inhibit?
123950.e: Cyanide binds to cytochrome c oxidase, complex IV. The electrons can no longer be transferred to oxygen, and cellular respiration comes to a halt.
123950.m: Cyanide blocks cytochrome c oxidase and therefore cellular respiration.

123951.q: Which mobile molecule transfers electrons from complexes I and II to complex III?
123951.e: Ubiquinone, also called coenzyme Q10, is fat-soluble and moves freely in the membrane. It shuttles electrons to complex III.
123951.m: Ubiquinone transports electrons within the membrane.

123952.q: According to current estimates, roughly how many ATP does the complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yield?
123952.e: Older textbooks give 36 to 38 ATP. Because the flow of protons has been measured more precisely, the figure today is around 30 to 32 ATP.
123952.m: A completely respired glucose yields around thirty ATP.

123953.q: Which molecules supply the electrons that flow through the respiratory chain?
123953.e: NADH and FADH2 are formed mainly in the citric acid cycle. They hand their electrons to the respiratory chain, whose energy is used to make ATP.
123953.m: NADH and FADH2 feed electrons into the respiratory chain.

123954.q: Where does the beta-oxidation of fatty acids mainly take place in humans?
123954.e: The fatty acids are broken down step by step in the mitochondria. Very long-chain fatty acids are first shortened in the peroxisomes.
123954.m: Beta-oxidation takes place in the mitochondria.

123955.q: Which product of beta-oxidation is then broken down further in the citric acid cycle?
123955.e: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids down into acetyl-CoA. This is broken down further into carbon dioxide in the citric acid cycle of the mitochondria.
123955.m: Fatty acids produce acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle.

123956.q: By how many carbon atoms is a fatty acid shortened in each round of beta-oxidation?
123956.e: Each round splits off a C2 unit as acetyl-CoA. The remaining chain starts the next round.
123956.m: Beta-oxidation shortens the fatty acid by two carbon atoms per round.

123957.q: How many molecules of acetyl-CoA are produced when palmitic acid with 16 carbon atoms is broken down completely?
123957.e: 16 carbon atoms divided by 2 gives 8 acetyl-CoA. Only 7 rounds are needed for this, because the last step yields two acetyl-CoA.
123957.m: Palmitic acid is broken down into eight acetyl-CoA.

123958.q: Where do the fatty acids broken down in beta-oxidation come from?
123958.e: Fats consist of glycerol and three fatty acids. When they are split, the fatty acids enter the mitochondria and are broken down there.
123958.m: Beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids from split fats.

123959.q: Where do the coenzymes NADH and FADH2 loaded in beta-oxidation hand over their electrons?
123959.e: NADH and FADH2 deliver their electrons to the respiratory chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. There most of the ATP is formed with them.
123959.m: The respiratory chain uses the electrons from beta-oxidation.

123960.q: When does the body rely particularly heavily on beta-oxidation?
a: During fasting and long endurance exercise
123960.e: When carbohydrate stores are low, the body increasingly draws on its fat reserves. The fatty acids are then broken down in beta-oxidation.
123960.m: During fasting and endurance sport, the body burns more fat.

123961.q: In which organ are ketone bodies formed?
123961.e: The liver cells form ketone bodies in their mitochondria, especially during fasting. They then release them into the blood.
123961.m: Ketone bodies are formed in the liver.

123962.q: Which ketone body is given off in the breath and has a fruity smell?
123962.e: Acetone forms through the spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate. It is volatile and is breathed out.
123962.m: Acetone gives the breath a fruity smell in ketosis.

123963.q: From which nutrient does the liver mainly form ketone bodies during fasting?
123963.e: During fasting, fatty acids are brought from the fatty tissue to the liver and broken down into acetyl-CoA. From this the liver builds the ketone bodies.
123963.m: Ketone bodies are made from fat.

123964.q: Why does the liver release ketone bodies into the blood during fasting?
a: As a source of energy for other organs
123964.e: The liver forms ketone bodies but cannot use them itself. In this way they are available as fuel for the heart, muscles and brain.
123964.m: The liver exports ketone bodies but does not use them itself.

123965.q: Which organ, which hardly uses fatty acids, covers a large part of its energy needs from ketone bodies during prolonged starvation?
123965.e: Fatty acids hardly cross the blood-brain barrier, but ketone bodies do. In this way the body saves glucose and spares the muscle proteins.
123965.m: During long fasting, the brain uses ketone bodies as a source of energy.

123966.q: What is the dangerous metabolic derailment called in which ketone bodies build up in the blood because of a lack of insulin?
123966.e: Without insulin, fatty acids are broken down on a massive scale and ketone bodies are formed. These acids lower the pH of the blood dangerously.
123966.m: A lack of insulin can lead to dangerous ketoacidosis.

123967.q: Which hormone situation promotes the formation of ketone bodies?
a: Little insulin and a lot of glucagon
A lot of insulin and little glucagon
A lot of insulin and a lot of glucagon
A lot of insulin after a meal
123967.e: Low insulin and high glucagon promote lipolysis and beta-oxidation in the liver. As a result, more ketone bodies are formed.
123967.m: More ketone bodies are formed when insulin is low and glucagon is high.

123968.q: Why does the body form more ketone bodies on a low-carbohydrate, ketogenic diet?
a: Without carbohydrates it breaks down more fat
Ketone bodies are found directly in vegetables
Protein is fermented into ketone bodies in the intestine
It then stores particularly large amounts of glycogen
123968.e: Without carbohydrates, the insulin level falls and the glycogen stores empty. The liver then breaks down more fatty acids and forms ketone bodies from them.
123968.m: Few carbohydrates put the body into ketosis.

123969.q: Why do people with ketoacidosis breathe very deeply and quickly?
a: To breathe out carbon dioxide and reduce the acid
Because the lungs form ketone bodies
123969.e: Carbon dioxide acts as an acid in the blood. If more of it is breathed out, the acidity falls. This deep breathing is called Kussmaul breathing.
123969.m: Kussmaul breathing is a response to metabolic acidosis.

123970.q: What does a permanently positive energy balance mean?
a: More energy is taken in than used
More energy is used than taken in
Intake and use are the same
123970.e: Excess energy is stored mainly as fat. In the long run, body weight therefore increases.
123970.m: Anyone who takes in more energy than they use gains weight.

123971.q: Which component makes up the largest part of daily energy use in adults who are not very active?
123971.e: With little exercise, the basal metabolic rate makes up around 60 to 70 per cent of total energy use. Activity and digestion share the rest.
123971.m: The basal metabolic rate is usually the biggest item in energy use.

123972.q: Which physical law forms the basis of every energy balance of the body?
123972.e: The first law states that energy is not lost but only converted. Energy taken in is used, stored or given off as heat.
123972.m: Energy is not lost in the body; it is only converted.

123973.q: A person has a basal metabolic rate of 1600 kcal and a PAL value of 1.5. What is their total energy use per day?
123973.e: Total energy use is the basal metabolic rate times the PAL value: 1600 kcal × 1.5 = 2400 kcal.
123973.m: Basal metabolic rate times PAL value gives total energy use.

123974.q: What does indirect calorimetry measure in order to determine energy use?
a: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide output
123974.e: From the gas exchange of breathing, you can calculate how much energy the body uses. For this the person wears a breathing mask, for example.
123974.m: Indirect calorimetry calculates energy use from the breathing gases.

123975.q: What respiratory quotient does the pure burning of carbohydrates have?
123975.e: With glucose, exactly one molecule of carbon dioxide is produced for each molecule of oxygen used. The ratio of CO2 output to O2 uptake is therefore 1.0.
123975.m: For carbohydrates, the respiratory quotient is one.

123976.q: For a week, someone takes in 500 kcal a day less than they use. How big is the energy deficit after this week?
123976.e: 7 days × 500 kcal = 3500 kcal. The body covers this deficit mainly from its energy stores.
123976.m: A daily deficit adds up over the week.

123977.q: How is the body mass index calculated?
a: Body mass in kg divided by the square of height in m
Body mass in kg divided by height in cm
Waist measurement divided by hip measurement
123977.e: The BMI has the unit kg per square metre. So the height is squared.
123977.m: For the BMI, you divide the weight by the height squared.

123978.q: What is the BMI of a person with a body mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m (rounded)?
123978.e: 1.80 m × 1.80 m = 3.24 m². 72 kg ÷ 3.24 m² gives around 22.2 kg/m².
123978.m: You get the BMI by dividing the weight by the height squared.

123979.q: A person weighs 90 kg and is 1.75 m tall. Which WHO category does their BMI fall into?
123979.e: 1.75 m × 1.75 m = 3.0625 m². 90 kg ÷ 3.0625 m² gives around 29.4, which is in the range from 25 to under 30.
123979.m: A BMI between 25 and 30 counts as overweight.

123980.q: Which BMI range counts as normal weight for adults according to the WHO?
123980.e: The WHO classifies adults with a BMI of 18.5 or more and under 25 as normal weight. Above that, overweight begins.
123980.m: Normal weight is a BMI between 18.5 and 25.

123981.q: From what BMI does the WHO speak of obesity in adults?
123981.e: A BMI of 30 or more counts as obesity. This is further divided into three classes.
123981.m: A BMI of 30 or more is called obesity.

123982.q: Which Belgian scholar developed the basis of the body mass index in the 19th century?
123982.e: The statistician Adolphe Quetelet found that the weight of adults increases roughly with the square of their height. The BMI used to be called the Quetelet index.
123982.m: The BMI goes back to Adolphe Quetelet.

123983.q: What is an important weakness of the body mass index?
a: It does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass
It can only be determined in a laboratory
It is only valid for children
It does not take body weight into account
123983.e: Very muscular athletes can have a high BMI without carrying much fat. The BMI does not show how fat is distributed either.
123983.m: The BMI says nothing about muscle content or fat distribution.

123984.q: How is the BMI assessed in children and teenagers?
a: With percentiles by age and sex
With the same fixed limits as for adults
Not at all, it cannot be calculated for them
123984.e: Because body shape changes a great deal during growth, the BMI is compared with children of the same age and sex. Percentile curves are used for this.
123984.m: In children, the BMI is assessed with percentile curves.

123986.q: Which distribution of fat is considered particularly bad for health?
a: A lot of fat in the abdomen around the organs
A lot of fat on the hips and thighs
A lot of fat on the forearms
Evenly distributed fat under the skin
123986.e: Visceral belly fat is metabolically active and releases substances that promote inflammation. It increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.
123986.m: Belly fat is particularly bad for health.

123987.q: Which metabolic disease is a common consequence of obesity?
123987.e: Being overweight promotes insulin resistance in the body's cells. This can develop into type 2 diabetes mellitus.
123987.m: Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes.

123988.q: Which hormone does fatty tissue produce to tell the brain how large the fat reserves are?
123988.e: Leptin has a satiating effect in the hypothalamus. In obesity the leptin level is high, but the brain often responds to it less strongly.
123988.m: Leptin from fatty tissue tells the brain about the fat reserves.

123989.q: Which joint disease is encouraged by severe overweight, especially in the knees?
123989.e: The extra load wears down the joint cartilage faster. That is why osteoarthritis of the knee is more common in obesity.
123989.m: Being overweight strains the knee joints and promotes osteoarthritis.

123990.q: Which breathing disorder during sleep occurs more often in obesity?
123990.e: Fatty tissue on the neck can narrow the upper airways during sleep. This leads to repeated pauses in breathing.
123990.m: Obesity encourages pauses in breathing at night.

123991.q: What is the surgery called that, in severe obesity, creates a gastric bypass, for example?
123991.e: Bariatric operations make the stomach smaller or shorten the path of food. They are an option in severe obesity when other measures are not enough.
123991.m: Bariatric surgery treats severe obesity with an operation.

123992.q: What is meant by activity energy expenditure?
a: Energy use beyond the basal metabolic rate
The energy use of the brain alone
123992.e: Activity energy expenditure covers the energy for movement, work, sport and other extra effort. Together with the basal metabolic rate, it gives total energy use.
123992.m: Activity energy expenditure is energy use above the basal metabolic rate.

123993.q: What does the unit 1 MET mean?
a: Energy use at rest while sitting
The energy in one gram of fat
123993.e: 1 MET corresponds roughly to resting energy use, around 1 kcal per kg of body mass per hour. An activity of 8 MET therefore uses eight times as much.
123993.m: One MET corresponds to energy use at rest.

123994.q: A person weighing 70 kg jogs for an hour at 8 MET. Roughly how much energy do they use if 1 MET is around 1 kcal per kg per hour?
123994.e: 8 kcal per kg per hour × 70 kg × 1 h = 560 kcal.
123994.m: You estimate energy use as MET times body mass times time.

124408.q: What colour is grade A on the Nutri-Score?
124408.e: A is dark green and stands for the best nutritional composition. E is red.
124408.m: A dark green A is the best Nutri-Score grade.

124786.q: What is the aim of the transition period after the season?
a: Physical and mental recovery while staying active
Increasing competition performance to the maximum
Taking part in as many extra competitions as possible
124786.e: After the competition period, the training load is greatly reduced. You stay active with varied, easy exercise and recharge your energy for the new season.
124786.m: The transition period is for recovery after the season.

124787.q: What does heart rate variability describe?
a: The variation in the intervals between heartbeats
The difference between resting and maximum heart rate
How loud the heart sounds are
The difference in pulse between the two arms
124787.e: The heart does not beat like a metronome. The time intervals between consecutive beats vary slightly, and this variation is called HRV.
124787.m: Heart rate variability measures how much the intervals between heartbeats vary.

124788.q: What does a resting HRV that is high compared with your own normal value usually indicate?
124788.e: A well-rested body reacts flexibly, and the intervals between beats vary more. Low values compared with your normal value, on the other hand, can point to stress or strain.
124788.m: A high resting HRV usually indicates good recovery.

124789.q: Through which cranial nerve does the parasympathetic nervous system mainly act on the heart?
124789.e: The vagus nerve slows the heartbeat and causes variations from beat to beat. Many HRV measures therefore reflect its activity.
124789.m: The vagus nerve calms the heart.

124790.q: What do many athletes use to measure their heart rate variability in everyday life?
a: A blood pressure cuff on the leg
124790.e: Chest straps and many smartwatches record the intervals between heartbeats very accurately. An app then calculates the HRV from them.
124790.m: Chest straps and smartwatches can measure HRV.

124791.q: Between which peaks on an ECG are the heartbeat intervals for HRV usually measured?
124791.e: The R wave is the highest and most clearly visible spike on the ECG. The interval between two R waves is called the RR interval.
124791.m: For HRV, the intervals between R waves are measured.

124792.q: When should HRV ideally be measured for planning training?
a: In the morning after waking, at rest
At any random time of day
124792.e: HRV values react strongly to movement, food and stress. The same conditions every morning make the measurements comparable from day to day.
124792.m: HRV is best measured in the morning under the same conditions.

124793.q: How does drinking alcohol the evening before usually affect HRV during the night?
124793.e: Alcohol puts strain on the body and dampens parasympathetic recovery during sleep. That is why HRV is usually lower than normal afterwards.

124794.q: How does the heart rate change during inhalation in respiratory sinus arrhythmia?
124794.e: When you breathe in, the influence of the parasympathetic nervous system decreases and the pulse rises. When you breathe out, it falls again, which contributes to HRV.
124794.m: When you breathe in, the heart rate rises slightly.

124795.q: Above which town is Magglingen, the headquarters of the Federal Office of Sport, located?
124795.e: Magglingen lies at the southern foot of the Jura, high above Lake Biel. The town of Biel is directly below it.

124796.q: Which federal department does the Federal Office of Sport (FOSPO) belong to?
a: Federal Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport
Federal Department of Economic Affairs, Education and Research
Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications
124796.e: Sport is part of the DDPS, which even has sport in its name. FOSPO is one of its federal offices.

124797.q: Which sports promotion programme for children and young people is run by the Federal Office of Sport?
124797.e: Jugend+Sport, or J+S for short, supports sports courses and camps in clubs and schools. It is the federal government's most important programme for children's and youth sport.
124797.m: Jugend+Sport is the federal sports promotion programme for young people.

124798.q: What is Magglingen, the home of the Federal Office of Sport, called in French?
124798.e: Magglingen lies on the language border in the Biel region, where German and French are spoken. The French name of the village is Macolin.
124798.m: Magglingen is called Macolin in French.

124799.q: Which university belongs to the Federal Office of Sport?
a: Swiss Federal Institute of Sport Magglingen
124799.e: The SFISM trains PE teachers and coaches, among others, and carries out research. It is part of the Federal Office of Sport itself.
124799.m: The Swiss Federal Institute of Sport Magglingen belongs to the Federal Office of Sport.

124800.q: In which place in Ticino does the Federal Office of Sport run a national youth sports centre?
124800.e: The Centro sportivo nazionale della gioventù in Tenero lies on Lake Maggiore. Many sports camps and training courses take place there.
124800.m: The national youth sports centre of the Confederation is in Tenero.

124801.q: Under what name was the federal school in Magglingen originally founded?
124801.e: The Federal Gymnastics and Sports School, or ETS for short, was the forerunner of today's Federal Office of Sport. The federal office and the sports university developed from it.
124801.m: The Federal Office of Sport grew out of the Federal Gymnastics and Sports School.

124802.q: Which federal law is the Confederation's promotion of sport mainly based on today?
124802.e: The Sport Promotion Act covers Jugend+Sport, school sport and elite sport, among other things. The Federal Office of Sport puts it into practice.
124802.m: Federal sports promotion is based on the Sport Promotion Act.

124803.q: Which deep abdominal muscle acts like a natural corset around the trunk?
124803.e: The transverse abdominal muscle, musculus transversus abdominis, wraps around the abdomen like a belt. It increases the pressure in the abdomen and so stabilises the spine.
124803.m: The transverse abdominal muscle stabilises the trunk like a corset.

124804.q: What is the static exercise called in which you hold your body straight on your forearms and toes?
124804.e: The plank, also called the forearm plank, trains all the trunk muscles. It is important that your head, back and legs form a straight line.
124804.m: The plank is a classic exercise for core stability.

124805.q: Which exercise mainly strengthens the back muscles of the trunk?
a: Back extensions lying on your front
124805.e: For back extensions you lie on your front and lift your upper body, or your arms and legs, slightly. The muscles along the spine do the work.
124805.m: Back extensions lying on your front strengthen the back muscles.

124806.q: Why is a stable trunk important for many sports?
a: It transfers force between the legs and arms
It lowers the maximum heart rate
124806.e: In throws, jumps or strikes, the force flows from the legs through the trunk to the arms. An unstable trunk lets energy go to waste.
124806.m: A stable trunk transfers force from the legs to the arms.

124807.q: Which English term is often used in training for the trunk muscles?
124807.e: Core means the centre. It refers to the muscles of the abdomen, back, hips and pelvis that stabilise the body in the middle.
124807.m: The trunk muscles are often called the core in training.

124808.q: Which poor posture is encouraged by weak abdominal muscles and a pelvis tilted forwards?
124808.e: When the pelvis tilts forwards, the curve of the lower spine increases. Strong abdominal and buttock muscles counteract this.
124808.m: Weak abdominal muscles can encourage a hollow back.

124809.q: Which breathing muscle forms the upper boundary of the abdominal cavity and helps stabilise the trunk?
124809.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the abdomen. Together with the abdominal muscles, it builds up pressure in the abdomen that supports the spine.
124809.m: The diaphragm helps with breathing and with stabilising the trunk.

124810.q: Which muscles does the side plank train in particular?
a: The side muscles of the trunk
124810.e: In the side plank you hold your body sideways on one forearm. Above all, the oblique abdominal muscles and the quadratus lumborum work hard.
124810.m: The side plank strengthens the side muscles of the trunk.

124811.q: Why is a resting ECG often done during sports medical examinations?
a: To detect heart disease and rhythm disorders
To measure the strength of the leg muscles
To measure the exact size of the lungs
124811.e: The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart. It can reveal certain heart conditions that may become dangerous during sport.
124811.m: A resting ECG can uncover dangerous heart problems in athletes.

124812.q: Which organisation publishes the worldwide list of prohibited substances and methods in sport every year?
124812.e: The World Anti-Doping Agency, WADA for short, draws up the prohibited list. National bodies and sports federations base their tests on it.
124812.m: WADA decides which substances are banned in sport.

a: A narrowing of the airways caused by physical exertion
An inflammation of the heart valves caused by sport
A hardening of the muscles after training
Feeling dizzy when standing up quickly
124813.e: In exercise-induced asthma, the bronchial tubes narrow during or after sport, often in cold, dry air. A good warm-up and medicine prescribed by a doctor help.
124813.m: Exercise-induced asthma is a narrowing of the airways caused by exertion.

124814.q: What should you do if an athlete collapses on the pitch and is no longer breathing normally?
a: Call 144, start chest compressions and use a defibrillator
Sit them up and give them water
Wait until they wake up by themselves
Drive them to hospital by car straight away
124814.e: In cardiac arrest, every minute counts. Calling for help, starting chest compressions at once and using a defibrillator greatly increase the chance of survival.
124814.m: In cardiac arrest: call for help, press, defibrillate.

124815.q: What is the name of Switzerland's national anti-doping foundation?
124815.e: Swiss Sport Integrity is the independent body for fighting doping and ethical violations in Swiss sport. It carries out doping tests.
124815.m: Swiss Sport Integrity fights doping in Swiss sport.

124816.q: What is a broken bone called that develops without an accident through repeated overuse?
124816.e: In a stress fracture, also called a fatigue fracture, many small loads cause fine cracks in the bone. Runners are often affected in the metatarsals or shin.
124816.m: Repeated overuse can lead to a stress fracture.

124817.q: What danger is there if you drink far too much plain water during a long run?
a: A dangerous lack of sodium in the blood
Low blood sugar due to a lack of protein
124817.e: Too much water dilutes the blood, while sodium is lost in sweat at the same time. This hyponatraemia can cause confusion and, in extreme cases, be life-threatening.
124817.m: Too much plain water during long exercise can lead to a lack of sodium.

124818.q: Why do many endurance athletes train at altitude for a while?
a: The lack of oxygen stimulates the production of red blood cells
The air at altitude contains more oxygen
124818.e: At altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen is lower. The body reacts by making more red blood cells and can then transport more oxygen.
124818.m: Altitude training encourages the production of red blood cells.

125113.q: What is the science called that studies biological rhythms such as the body clock?
125113.e: The word comes from the Greek “chronos” (time). Chronobiology studies things such as the sleep-wake rhythm, jet lag and shift work.

125114.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the body clock in the body's cells last?
125114.e: The body clock is based on genes that switch themselves on and off in a feedback loop. One cycle lasts about a day, hence the name circadian rhythm.
125114.m: The body clock ticks in a rhythm of about 24 hours.

125115.q: What do single nerve cells of the suprachiasmatic nucleus show when they are kept in a cell culture?
a: They keep their own daily rhythm.
125115.e: Even when isolated, the activity and gene reading of these cells vary with a period of about 24 hours. So the clock is in every single cell.
125115.m: Single cells of the master clock keep ticking even on their own.

125116.q: Which feeling becomes stronger as adenosine builds up in the brain during the day?
125116.e: The longer you are awake, the more adenosine builds up in the brain. It dampens the nerve cells and creates sleep pressure.

125117.q: What is the time from falling asleep to the start of the first REM phase called?
125117.e: REM latency is fairly long in healthy people, because the non-REM stages come first. A very short REM latency can point to an illness.
125117.m: REM latency measures the time until the first REM phase.

125118.q: Someone spends 8 hours in bed and sleeps for 6 of them. What is their sleep efficiency?
125118.e: Sleep efficiency is the time asleep divided by the time in bed. 6 divided by 8 gives 0.75, which is 75 per cent.
125118.m: Sleep efficiency compares the time asleep with the time in bed.

125119.q: What is measured with an EEG in a sleep laboratory?
125119.e: The electroencephalogram uses electrodes on the scalp to measure the electrical activity of the brain. This shows the stages of sleep.
125119.m: The EEG shows the brain waves during sleep.

125120.q: In which sleep phase is it hardest to wake someone up?
a: In light sleep shortly before waking
125120.e: In deep sleep, the brain is greatly slowed down. People woken from it are often especially groggy.
125120.m: Deep sleep is the hardest to wake up from.

125121.q: What is the temporary grogginess and reduced performance straight after waking up called?
125121.e: Sleep inertia can last from a few minutes to over half an hour. It is particularly strong when you are woken from deep sleep.
125121.m: Right after waking up, sleep inertia dampens performance.

125122.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle of non-REM and REM sleep last?
125122.e: One cycle lasts about 90 minutes. During a night you therefore go through four to six of these cycles.
125122.m: A sleep cycle lasts about one and a half hours.

125123.q: How does the proportion of REM sleep change during the night?
a: It stays the same all night
It only occurs in the first hour
125123.e: In the first half of the night, deep sleep dominates. Towards morning the REM phases get longer, which is why you often remember dreams from shortly before waking.
125123.m: REM sleep gets longer towards morning.

125124.q: Why do you hardly move in REM sleep despite vivid dreams?
a: The skeletal muscles are largely paralysed
The brain is completely switched off then
The heart does not beat then
You are unconscious as under anaesthetic
125124.e: In REM sleep, the muscles are strongly inhibited and only the eyes and breathing muscles move. This stops you acting out your dreams with real movements.
125124.m: In REM sleep the muscles are almost paralysed.

125125.q: In sleep medicine, what is meant by an arousal?
a: A brief waking reaction on the EEG lasting at least 3 seconds
Waking up completely in the morning
125125.e: An arousal is a sudden switch to faster brain waves for a few seconds. People often do not notice these brief waking reactions.
125125.m: An arousal is a brief, often unnoticed waking reaction.

125126.q: How is airflow measured in a sleep laboratory?
a: With sensors at the nose and mouth
With a clip on the earlobe
With a thermometer in the ear
125126.e: Small sensors in front of the nose and mouth record the airflow or changes in temperature during breathing. This reveals pauses in breathing and shallow breathing.
125126.m: Airflow is measured at the nose and mouth.

125127.q: Why are leg movements also recorded in a sleep laboratory?
a: To identify restless legs as a cause of poor sleep
125127.e: Some people move their legs again and again in their sleep and briefly wake up as a result. Electrodes on the legs make these movements visible.

125128.q: What is it called when many people sleep worse during their first night in a sleep laboratory?
125128.e: The unfamiliar surroundings and the cables disturb sleep on the first night. That is why measurements are sometimes taken over two nights.
125128.m: People often sleep worse on their first night in a sleep laboratory.

a: A marked flattening of breathing with a drop in oxygen or a waking reaction
A complete stop in breathing lasting over a minute
125129.e: In a hypopnoea, the airflow is greatly reduced but not completely interrupted. Like apnoea, it counts as a breathing disorder during sleep.
125129.m: A hypopnoea is a strong flattening of breathing.

125130.q: Which treatment is most commonly used for obstructive sleep apnoea?
a: A breathing mask with slight positive pressure (CPAP)
125130.e: The CPAP machine blows air with slight positive pressure into the airways through a mask. This keeps the throat open during sleep.
125130.m: A CPAP mask keeps the airways open during sleep.

125131.q: What is the main feature of narcolepsy?
a: Severe daytime sleepiness with sudden falling asleep
Loud snoring with pauses in breathing
125131.e: People with narcolepsy can hardly stay awake during the day and sometimes fall asleep in the middle of an activity. The cause is a disorder in the brain's control of sleeping and waking.
125131.m: Narcolepsy causes severe sleepiness during the day.

125132.q: On which day of the week is the conflict between the body clock and the alarm time usually greatest with social jet lag?
125132.e: After sleeping late at the weekend, the body clock has shifted later. On Monday morning the alarm then rings especially early in your internal night.
125132.m: Monday morning is especially hard with social jet lag.

125133.q: What is the aim of sleep restriction in the treatment of insomnia?
a: To match the time in bed to the actual sleep time in order to increase sleep pressure
To spend as many hours as possible in bed
To sleep only during the day
To stay awake all night every night
125133.e: People who lie awake in bed for a long time sleep in fragments. Shortening the time in bed increases sleep pressure, and sleep becomes deeper and more continuous.
125133.m: Sleep restriction shortens the time in bed so that sleep becomes deeper.

125134.q: What is recommended about eating in the evening for a good night's sleep?
a: No heavy meals shortly before going to bed
A big meal right before going to sleep
Eating nothing at all after midday
Only very spicy food in the evening
125134.e: A heavy meal keeps the digestion busy and can make it harder to fall asleep. A light meal a few hours before sleeping is better.
125134.m: A heavy evening meal shortly before sleeping disturbs your night's rest.

125135.q: What does the word “circadian” literally mean?
125135.e: The word comes from the Latin “circa” (about) and “dies” (day). It refers to biological rhythms with a period of about 24 hours.
125135.m: Circadian rhythms last about a day.

125136.q: On average, how long is the internal period of the human clock when all external time cues are missing?
125136.e: Without time cues, the body clock of most people runs a little longer than 24 hours. That is why it has to be adjusted to the day anew every day.
125136.m: The human body clock usually runs a little slower than the 24-hour day.

125137.q: In which model organism were the molecular mechanisms of the body clock researched that were awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2017?
125137.e: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young studied clock genes in the fruit fly Drosophila. For this they received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
125137.m: The molecular body clock was first decoded in the fruit fly.

125138.q: Which hormone does the body typically release in particularly large amounts shortly after waking in the morning?
125138.e: The cortisol level rises in the second half of the night and peaks shortly after waking. Cortisol helps to provide energy for the day.
125138.m: Cortisol reaches its peak in the morning after waking.

125139.q: When does the core body temperature of a person with a normal sleep rhythm typically reach its minimum?
a: In the early hours of the morning
125139.e: Core temperature follows a circadian rhythm and is lowest in the second half of the night, a few hours before waking. It is highest in the late afternoon.
125139.m: Body temperature is lowest in the early hours of the morning.

125140.q: What do you call a biological rhythm that continues with its own period without external time cues?
125140.e: In isolation experiments without daylight and clocks, the rhythm runs freely with its own period. It then shifts a little each day compared with clock time.
125140.m: A free-running rhythm follows only its own period.

125141.q: Why is adjusting to the time difference after an eastward flight usually harder than after a westward one?
a: The body clock has to be put forward, which is harder.
There is less sunlight during the day in the east.
The air pressure in the plane is lower when flying east.
Eastward flights always take much longer.
125141.e: Because the internal period is usually a little longer than 24 hours, it is easier to shift the clock later. After an eastward flight, however, you have to sleep earlier, which means putting the clock forward.
125141.m: Flying east requires putting the body clock forward and is therefore harder.

125142.q: What are biological rhythms called whose period is much shorter than a day, such as the sleep cycle at night?
125142.e: Ultradian rhythms repeat several times a day. Infradian rhythms, on the other hand, last longer than a day, and circannual ones about a year.
125142.m: Ultradian rhythms run several times a day.

125143.q: What does the name “suprachiasmatic” refer to?
a: Its position above the crossing of the optic nerves
Its connection to the spinal cord
125143.e: “Supra” means above, and the “optic chiasm” is where the optic nerves cross. The nucleus lies directly above it and so easily receives signals from the eyes.
125143.m: The suprachiasmatic nucleus lies above the crossing of the optic nerves.

125144.q: Where does the master clock in the brain get the information about whether it is day or night?
a: From the retina of the eyes
From the skin via the temperature
125144.e: A special nerve pathway leads directly from the retina to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. It reports brightness, not images.
125144.m: Light reaches the master clock through the eyes.

125145.q: Which light shifts the body clock particularly strongly in the evening, for example from a mobile phone screen?
125145.e: Special cells in the retina react mainly to blue light and report it to the body clock. In the evening it inhibits the production of melatonin and delays falling asleep.
125145.m: Blue light in the evening shifts the body clock.

125146.q: What happens in laboratory animals when the suprachiasmatic nucleus is destroyed?
a: The sleep-wake rhythm loses its daily order.
The animals no longer sleep at all.
Their body temperature rises sharply for good.
125146.e: Without the master clock, sleep and activity are spread randomly over day and night. The animals still sleep, but no longer in a daily rhythm.
125146.m: Without the suprachiasmatic nucleus, there is no orderly daily rhythm.

125147.q: What did transplant experiments show in which hamsters without their own master clock received the suprachiasmatic nucleus of another animal?
a: The animals took on the rhythm of the donor animal.
The animals had no rhythm at all.
The animals always rejected the tissue.
125147.e: After the transplant, the recipients showed the donor's period, not their own previous period. This proved that the nucleus itself sets the pace.
125147.m: A transplanted suprachiasmatic nucleus brings its own rhythm with it.

125148.q: What are the clocks in organs such as the liver or heart called that are coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus?
125148.e: Almost every cell in the body has its own molecular clock. The master clock in the brain coordinates these peripheral clocks with each other.
125148.m: Peripheral clocks in the organs are coordinated by the master clock in the brain.

125149.q: The breakdown of which molecule is the main source of adenosine in cells?
125149.e: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy carrier of the cells. When it is used up, adenosine is produced in several steps.
125149.m: Adenosine is a breakdown product of the energy carrier ATP.

125150.q: How does caffeine make you more alert?
a: It breaks down adenosine in the blood.
It activates the suprachiasmatic nucleus directly.
125150.e: Caffeine resembles adenosine and occupies its receptors without activating them. As a result, the tiredness signal gets through less well.
125150.m: Caffeine blocks the docking sites for adenosine.

125151.q: Why can a coffee in the evening make it harder to fall asleep?
a: Caffeine blocks the tiredness signal of adenosine
125151.e: Caffeine occupies the adenosine receptors in the brain. Because it works for hours, the tiredness signal gets through less well in the evening.
125151.m: Caffeine in the evening can disturb sleep.

125152.q: According to the two-process model, which two processes control when we sleep?
a: Sleep pressure and the body clock
125152.e: Sleep pressure rises the longer we are awake, and the body clock follows a daily rhythm. The model was developed by the Zurich researcher Alexander Borbély.
125152.m: Sleep pressure and the body clock together determine sleep.

125153.q: What does “Process S” stand for in the two-process model of sleep regulation?
125153.e: Process S rises the longer you are awake and falls during sleep. Process C, by contrast, is the circadian rhythm of the body clock.
125153.m: Process S describes the sleep pressure that rises the longer you are awake.

125154.q: Which measuring method is used to record brain waves during sleep?
125154.e: In an EEG, electrodes on the scalp measure the electrical activity of the brain. This shows sleep phases such as deep sleep and REM sleep.
125154.m: The EEG shows the brain waves.

125155.q: Roughly what is the half-life of caffeine in healthy adults?
125155.e: After about 5 hours, half of the caffeine has been broken down, although the values vary greatly from person to person. A coffee in the late afternoon can therefore still affect sleep.
125155.m: Caffeine keeps working for many hours after you drink it.

125156.q: Which two building blocks make up the nucleoside adenosine?
125156.e: Adenosine consists of the base adenine bound to the sugar ribose. When phosphate groups are added, nucleotides are formed.
125156.m: Adenosine is made of adenine and ribose.

125157.q: How many non-REM stages does the classification now used by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine distinguish?
125157.e: The AASM distinguishes the stages N1, N2 and N3 as well as REM sleep. N3 corresponds to deep sleep.
125157.m: Today non-REM sleep is divided into three stages.

125158.q: What does pulse oximetry measure during a sleep study?
a: The oxygen saturation of the blood
The carbon dioxide content of the room air
The brain waves in deep sleep
125158.e: A sensor on the finger uses light to measure what percentage of the haemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Drops in saturation point to pauses in breathing.
125158.m: Pulse oximetry measures the oxygen saturation in the blood.

125159.q: Which sleep phase can be recognised in polysomnography by rapid eye movements and relaxed muscles?
125159.e: REM stands for “Rapid Eye Movement”. In this phase you dream especially vividly, while the body's muscles are almost paralysed.
125159.m: In REM sleep the eyes move quickly.

125160.q: Which sleep disorder can be easily recognised with video polysomnography because those affected act out their dreams physically?
125160.e: In REM sleep behaviour disorder, the normal muscle paralysis during REM sleep is missing. Those affected hit or kick in their dreams, which is visible on video and in the EMG.
125160.m: In REM sleep behaviour disorder, dreams are acted out.

125161.q: What is typically missing in home polygraphy compared with polysomnography in a sleep laboratory?
125161.e: Polygraphy mainly records breathing and oxygen, but usually no EEG. That is why it cannot determine the stages of sleep.
125161.m: Home polygraphy usually does not measure brain waves.

125162.q: From what duration does a pause in breathing during sleep count as an apnoea?
125162.e: An apnoea is a pause in breathing of 10 seconds or more. Shorter pauses do not count as an apnoea.
125162.m: An apnoea lasts at least ten seconds.

125163.q: What does the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) indicate?
a: The number of breathing pauses and shallow breaths per hour of sleep
The length of the longest pause in breathing
The lowest oxygen value of the night
The number of snoring noises per night
125163.e: The AHI counts apnoeas and hypopnoeas and divides them by the hours of sleep. It is used to classify how severe the condition is.
125163.m: The AHI counts the breathing disturbances per hour of sleep.

125164.q: Which risk factor particularly encourages obstructive sleep apnoea?
125164.e: Fatty tissue around the neck narrows the upper airways. During sleep the muscles relax and the throat collapses more easily.
125164.m: Being overweight increases the risk of sleep apnoea.

125165.q: How does obstructive sleep apnoea differ from central sleep apnoea?
a: In the obstructive type the upper airways collapse even though there is breathing effort.
In the obstructive type there is no drive to breathe from the brain at all.
The obstructive type only occurs while awake.
The obstructive type only affects the lungs themselves.
125165.e: In the obstructive type, the body tries to breathe but the throat is blocked. In the central type, the breathing centre briefly sends no signals.
125165.m: In obstructive sleep apnoea, no air moves despite breathing effort.

125166.q: Which main daytime symptom often occurs with untreated sleep apnoea?
a: An increased urge to move the legs
