125166.e: Because of the many brief waking reactions, sleep is not restful. Those affected easily nod off during the day, which is dangerous when driving, for example.
125166.m: Sleep apnoea often makes people very sleepy during the day.

125167.q: Which cardiovascular disease is encouraged by untreated obstructive sleep apnoea?
125167.e: With every pause in breathing, the body reacts with a stress response and a rise in blood pressure. Over the years this increases the risk of permanent high blood pressure.
125167.m: Untreated sleep apnoea increases the risk of high blood pressure.

125168.q: Which alternative to mask therapy is often used for mild to moderate obstructive sleep apnoea?
125168.e: The splint pushes the lower jaw slightly forwards during sleep. This keeps the throat more open.
125168.m: A lower jaw splint can keep the airways open during sleep.

125169.q: In narcolepsy, what is meant by cataplexy?
a: A sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions
125169.e: In cataplexy, the muscles suddenly go limp, for example when laughing or being surprised. The person stays conscious throughout.
125169.m: Cataplexy is a loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions.

125170.q: What is the job of the messenger substance that is missing in type 1 narcolepsy?
a: It keeps us steadily awake during the day
125170.e: In type 1 narcolepsy, nerve cells in the hypothalamus that produce orexin are lost. Without this messenger substance, the brain easily tips from waking into sleep.
125170.m: In type 1 narcolepsy, a messenger substance that keeps us awake is missing.

125171.q: Which test in a sleep laboratory measures how quickly someone falls asleep on several occasions during the day?
125171.e: In the multiple sleep latency test, the person is allowed to lie down several times spread over the day. Short times to fall asleep and early REM phases point to narcolepsy.
125171.m: The multiple sleep latency test measures the tendency to fall asleep during the day.

125172.q: What is typical of narcolepsy on a sleep EEG?
a: REM sleep starts soon after falling asleep.
The eyes do not move at all during sleep.
125172.e: Normally the first REM sleep only comes after about 90 minutes. In narcolepsy it often occurs within 15 minutes of falling asleep.
125172.m: In narcolepsy, REM sleep comes unusually early.

125173.q: What are vivid, dream-like sensations when falling asleep called, which are common in narcolepsy?
125173.e: Hypnagogic hallucinations occur during the transition from waking to sleeping. They arise because elements of REM sleep intrude into the waking state.
125173.m: Hypnagogic hallucinations occur when falling asleep.

125174.q: What is the experience called of briefly being unable to move a single muscle on waking, while fully conscious?
125174.e: In sleep paralysis, the muscle paralysis of REM sleep lasts briefly after waking up. It is more common in narcolepsy, but also happens to healthy people.
125174.m: In sleep paralysis you are awake but briefly unable to move.

125175.q: After which vaccination campaign was a rise in narcolepsy cases observed in some countries?
125175.e: Especially in Scandinavia, more cases of narcolepsy occurred after the swine flu vaccine Pandemrix. An autoimmune reaction in genetically susceptible people is suspected.
125175.m: After the 2009 swine flu vaccination, more narcolepsy cases occurred in some countries.

125176.q: What are people with an early chronotype called in everyday language?
125176.e: Larks wake up early and get tired early. Owls, on the other hand, are active late and like to sleep in.
125176.m: Larks are awake early, owls are active late.

125177.q: What does the term chronotype describe?
a: Whether someone tends to be active early or late
How long someone can hold their breath
125177.e: The chronotype describes your personal body clock. Larks are awake early, owls only really come alive in the evening.
125177.m: The chronotype describes whether you are an early riser or a night person.

125178.q: On which days does your own chronotype show most clearly?
a: On free days without an alarm clock
On school days with an early alarm
On days after a long journey
125178.e: Without an alarm, you sleep according to your own body clock. That is why researchers use sleep times on free days to determine the chronotype.
125178.m: Free days without an alarm show your true chronotype.

125179.q: At what age is the average person's chronotype at its latest?
125179.e: During adolescence, the chronotype shifts later and later. Around the age of 20 it is at its latest and then slowly becomes earlier again.
125179.m: Around the age of twenty, people have their latest chronotype.

125180.q: How does the chronotype typically change in later adulthood?
a: It stays exactly the same from age 20.
125180.e: On average, older people go to bed earlier and wake up earlier. This reflects the body clock shifting earlier.
125180.m: In old age the chronotype becomes earlier.

125181.q: Which external stimulus sets the human body clock most strongly?
125181.e: Light in the morning resets the body clock every day. People who get a lot of light in the evening and little in the morning tend to become late chronotypes.
125181.m: Light is the most important time cue for the body clock.

125182.q: What is the disorder called in which someone can only ever fall asleep and wake up very late?
125182.e: In delayed sleep phase syndrome, the body clock is shifted much later. Those affected often only fall asleep after midnight and find it hard to get out of bed in the morning.
125182.m: In delayed sleep phase syndrome, the body clock is shifted much later.

125183.q: Among other things, what does a person's chronotype depend on?
a: Only on the month they were born
125183.e: Twin and family studies show that the chronotype is partly inherited. Age and light also play a big role.

125184.q: What is meant by social jet lag?
a: The difference in mid-sleep time between working days and free days
Lack of sleep after a party
The time difference between two countries
125184.e: With social jet lag, the body clock has to live against its own rhythm because of school or work. At the weekend it then returns to its later times.
125184.m: Social jet lag happens when social schedules and the body clock do not match.

125185.q: On average, who is particularly affected by social jet lag?
125185.e: Teenagers have a late chronotype but have to go to school early. This gap between body clock and timetable is especially large for them.
125185.m: Teenagers suffer particularly often from social jet lag.

125186.q: A person sleeps from 11 pm to 6.30 am on working days and from 1 am to 10 am on free days. How big is their social jet lag?
125186.e: The mid-sleep point on working days is at 2.45 am, on free days at 5.30 am. The difference is 2 hours 45 minutes.
125186.m: Social jet lag is calculated from the difference between the two mid-sleep points.

125187.q: Someone sleeps from midnight to 7 am during the week and from 2 am to 11 am at the weekend. How big is the social jet lag?
125187.e: The mid-sleep point is at 3.30 am during the week and at 6.30 am at the weekend. The difference is 3 hours.
125187.m: For social jet lag you compare the mid-sleep points, not the length of sleep.

125188.q: Why do many people sleep much longer at the weekend than during the week?
a: They are catching up on sleep lost during the week.
The night is astronomically longer at the weekend.
The body basically needs twice as much sleep at the weekend.
Caffeine does not work at the weekend.
125188.e: During the week, the alarm clock shortens sleep, because you have to get up early despite a late body clock. At the weekend the sleep debt is partly made up.
125188.m: Sleeping in for a long time at the weekend often shows a sleep debt.

125189.q: Which health risk has social jet lag been linked to in studies?
a: An increased risk of being overweight
125189.e: Observational studies found that people with large social jet lag more often had a higher body mass index. Mood and performance can also suffer.
125189.m: Large social jet lag is more often linked to being overweight.

125190.q: Which measure can help reduce the social jet lag of a late chronotype?
a: Plenty of daylight in the morning
Bright screen light late in the evening
Sleeping until midday at the weekend
Drinking lots of coffee in the evening
125190.e: Morning light shifts the body clock earlier, so you get tired earlier in the evening. Light in the evening has the opposite effect.
125190.m: Morning light helps to set the body clock earlier.

125191.q: Which system in the brain does a job that the lymphatic system does in the rest of the body?
125191.e: The brain has no classic lymphatic vessels in its tissue. Instead, the glymphatic system, described in 2012, flushes out waste with brain fluid.
125191.m: The glymphatic system is the brain's rubbish collection.

125192.q: Where does the name “glymphatic” come from?
125192.e: The system depends on glial cells and does a job in the brain that the lymphatic system does elsewhere. The made-up word comes from this.
125192.m: The name glymphatic combines glial cells and the lymphatic system.

125193.q: What main job is attributed to the glymphatic system?
a: Flushing waste out of the brain
Producing hormones in the pituitary gland
Carrying nerve signals to the muscles
125193.e: Brain fluid flows through the tissue and carries away metabolic waste. In this way the brain is cleaned, even though it has no classic lymphatic vessels in its tissue.
125193.m: The glymphatic system flushes waste out of the brain.

125194.q: According to studies in mice, when does the glymphatic system work hardest?
125194.e: During sleep, the space between the brain cells gets much larger. This lets the fluid flow through the tissue much more easily.
125194.m: The brain is cleaned especially well during sleep.

125195.q: Which fluid flows through the brain tissue in the glymphatic system?
125195.e: Cerebrospinal fluid flows along the blood vessels into the tissue and mixes with the fluid between the cells. It then leaves the brain along the veins.
125195.m: In the glymphatic system, cerebrospinal fluid flows through the brain.

125196.q: Along which structures does brain fluid flow into the brain tissue in the glymphatic system?
125196.e: Brain fluid flows into the tissue in spaces around the arteries. Waste then leaves the brain along the veins.
125196.m: The glymphatic system uses the spaces around the blood vessels.

125197.q: Which cells form the walls of the channels along the blood vessels in the glymphatic system with their extensions?
125197.e: Astrocytes are glial cells that surround the blood vessels with their end feet. They form the outer boundary of the spaces in which the cerebrospinal fluid flows.
125197.m: Astrocytes wrap around the blood vessels of the brain.

125198.q: Which waste substance linked to Alzheimer's disease is removed by the glymphatic system?
125198.e: In Alzheimer's disease, beta-amyloid builds up as plaques. Studies show that more of it is washed out during sleep.
125198.m: The glymphatic system also removes beta-amyloid from the brain.

125199.q: Which bedroom temperature is usually recommended for a good night's sleep?
125199.e: As you fall asleep, your body temperature drops slightly. A fairly cool room supports this process.
125199.m: A cool bedroom helps you sleep well.

125200.q: How does alcohol in the evening affect sleep?
a: It makes falling asleep easier but disturbs sleep later on.
It improves sleep all night long.
It has no effect on sleep at all.
125200.e: Alcohol has a calming effect at first, but it suppresses REM sleep. In the second half of the night, sleep becomes restless and you wake up more often.
125200.m: Alcohol makes you tired but makes your sleep worse.

125201.q: Which rule about sleep times is one of the most important sleep hygiene recommendations?
a: Regular times for going to bed and getting up, even at the weekend
Going to bed at a different time every day
Sleeping until the afternoon at the weekend if possible
Only going to bed when completely exhausted
125201.e: Fixed times stabilise the body clock. Big differences between weekdays and the weekend throw the rhythm into confusion.
125201.m: Regular sleep times strengthen the body clock.

125202.q: What is the method called in which the bed is only used for sleeping, so that it becomes linked with sleep again?
125202.e: In stimulus control, the bed should not be used for working, eating or watching TV. This way the brain learns to connect bed and sleep again.
125202.m: In stimulus control, the bed is used only for sleeping.

125203.q: What is recommended if you cannot fall asleep after about 20 minutes in bed?
a: Get up and do something calm until you feel tired
Stay lying there and look at the clock
125203.e: Lying awake and brooding for a long time links the bed with being awake. It is better to get up and only go back when you feel sleepy.
125203.m: If you cannot fall asleep, it is better to get up for a while.

125204.q: What is true about sport in connection with good sleep?
a: Regular exercise helps, but intense sport just before sleeping tends not to.
Sport should always be done just before falling asleep.
Exercise has no influence on sleep.
125204.e: Physical activity during the day improves sleep quality. However, very strenuous training shortly before going to bed can make it harder to fall asleep.
125204.m: Regular exercise during the day helps you sleep.

125205.q: What does the name restless legs syndrome describe?
a: Legs that will not keep still
125205.e: Restless means unable to keep still. Those affected feel a strong urge to move their legs, especially when resting.
125205.m: Restless legs means legs that will not keep still.

125206.q: What is typical of the symptoms of restless legs syndrome?
a: They occur at rest and in the evening and get better with movement.
They disappear immediately when lying down.
They only affect the hands in the morning.
125206.e: Those affected feel a tormenting urge to move with unpleasant sensations in the legs. Walking or stretching relieves the symptoms for a while.
125206.m: In restless legs syndrome, the legs feel the urge to move when at rest.

125207.q: Which deficiency can trigger or worsen restless legs syndrome?
125207.e: The brain needs iron to make dopamine. That is why the ferritin level is often checked in those affected and iron is given as a supplement.
125207.m: Iron deficiency can make restless legs worse.

125208.q: Which messenger substance in the brain is closely linked to restless legs syndrome?
125208.e: In restless legs syndrome, signal transmission with dopamine in the brain is disturbed. That is why medicines that act like dopamine often help.
125208.m: Dopamine plays an important role in restless legs syndrome.

125209.q: Why are people with restless legs syndrome often tired during the day?
a: The symptoms disturb falling asleep and sleep itself
The legs use too much oxygen at night
The illness makes them sleep too long
125209.e: The symptoms occur in the evening and at rest. Anyone who has to keep getting up and moving their legs finds it hard to fall asleep and often wakes up.
125209.m: Restless legs rob many sufferers of their sleep.

125210.q: What do the partners of people with restless legs syndrome often notice at night?
a: Regular twitching of the legs during sleep
125210.e: Many sufferers move their legs at regular intervals in their sleep. These movements can briefly wake them up.
125210.m: In restless legs syndrome, the legs often twitch during sleep too.

125211.q: In which chronic illness does secondary restless legs syndrome occur particularly often?
125211.e: People with severe kidney failure, for example those on dialysis, often have restless legs. This is then called secondary restless legs syndrome.
125211.m: People with kidney disease often suffer from secondary restless legs syndrome.

125212.q: How is restless legs syndrome mainly diagnosed?
a: From the typical symptoms described in conversation
With an X-ray of the legs
With a blood test for a particular virus
125212.e: The diagnosis is based on set clinical criteria such as the urge to move, rest and worsening in the evening. Blood tests and sleep laboratories are only used in addition.
125212.m: Restless legs syndrome is mainly recognised from the symptoms.

125400.q: Where does the energy stored in biomass originally come from?
a: From geothermal heat deep inside the Earth
From nuclear fission in the ground
125400.e: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy and store it in sugar, starch and cellulose. This energy is released again when it is burnt.

125510.q: What is the WHO's international classification system called, in which depression is also described as an illness?
125510.e: The ICD (International Classification of Diseases) is the diagnostic system of the World Health Organization. The DSM, by contrast, comes from the American Psychiatric Association.
125510.m: The ICD is the WHO's list of diseases.

125511.q: According to ICD-10, which feature is one of the main symptoms of depression?
a: Greatly increased need for sleep after sport
125511.e: The main symptoms include low mood, loss of interest and enjoyment, and reduced drive. Increased drive and ideas of grandeur are more typical of mania.
125511.m: Loss of enjoyment is a core symptom of depression.

125512.q: What does the technical term “anhedonia” mean?
a: Restlessness in the legs while sleeping
125512.e: Anhedonia comes from Greek and means roughly “without pleasure or joy”. It is a common symptom of depression.
125512.m: Anhedonia means you can no longer feel pleasure.

125513.q: According to ICD-10, how long must the symptoms last at least for a depressive episode to be diagnosed?
125513.e: For a depressive episode, ICD-10 requires a duration of at least about two weeks. Short phases of sadness are not yet depression.
125513.m: A depressive episode lasts at least about two weeks.

125514.q: What is the mental illness called in which depressive and manic phases alternate?
125514.e: In bipolar disorder, phases of low mood alternate with phases of exaggerated mood and activity. It used to be called manic depression.
125514.m: In bipolar disorder, depression and mania alternate.

125515.q: What is a chronic, milder depressive low mood that lasts for years called?
125515.e: Dysthymia is a lasting but less severe depressive low mood over at least two years. Cyclothymia, by contrast, is a mild form of changing moods.
125515.m: Dysthymia is a long-lasting mild depression.

125516.q: Which messenger substance in the brain do the commonly prescribed SSRI antidepressants mainly act on?
125516.e: SSRI stands for “selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors”. They prevent serotonin from being quickly taken back into the nerve cell.
125516.m: SSRIs act on the messenger substance serotonin.

125517.q: Which treatment is often used for seasonal affective disorder (“winter depression”)?
125517.e: In winter depression, the lack of light in the dark season plays a role. Bright light from special lamps can ease the symptoms.
125517.m: Light therapy often helps against winter depression.

125518.q: When does the mood-lifting effect of antidepressants typically begin?
a: Often only after a few weeks
125518.e: Antidepressants usually work with a delay, often only after two to four weeks. That is why patience is important, and you should not stop taking them on your own.
125518.m: Antidepressants usually only work after a few weeks.

a: Fear of only one particular animal
Fear of being judged by others
125519.e: In panic disorder, panic attacks happen again and again, apparently for no reason. Often a fear of the next attack develops as well.
125519.m: Panic disorder shows itself through repeated unexpected panic attacks.

125520.q: What are people with agoraphobia typically afraid of?
a: Places from which escape seems difficult
125520.e: Agoraphobia originally means “fear of the marketplace”. People fear crowds, public transport or places where help or escape seems difficult.
125520.m: People with agoraphobia avoid places that would be hard to escape from.

125521.q: Which anxiety disorder is mainly characterised by fear of being judged by other people?
125521.e: In social phobia, people fear embarrassing themselves or being judged negatively. Situations such as giving talks or conversations are therefore often avoided.
125521.m: Social phobia is the fear of being judged negatively by others.

125522.q: What is typical of generalised anxiety disorder?
a: Lasting worries about many areas of life
125522.e: In generalised anxiety disorder, thoughts revolve around many everyday worries for months. Tension, restlessness and sleep problems are often added.
125522.m: In generalised anxiety disorder, you constantly worry about many things.

125523.q: What is the abnormal fear of narrow, enclosed spaces called?
125523.e: Claustrophobia comes from the Latin “claustrum”, meaning “a closed place”. People affected avoid lifts or narrow tubes, for example.
125523.m: Claustrophobia is the fear of enclosed spaces.

125524.q: Which method is considered particularly effective for specific phobias?
125524.e: In exposure therapy, you face the feared situation step by step with support. You learn that the fear goes down again by itself.
125524.m: For phobias, gradually facing the fear helps.

125525.q: Which part of the nervous system triggers typical physical reactions to fear, such as a racing heart and sweating?
125525.e: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for fight or flight. Heartbeat and breathing speed up, and you sweat.
125525.m: The sympathetic nervous system controls the fight-or-flight response.

125526.q: Why does avoidance behaviour strengthen a fear in the long run?
a: You never experience that the danger does not happen
You move too little in everyday life
It makes you sleep too much
It makes you eat too much sugar
125526.e: Avoiding a situation brings short-term relief. But you never find out that what you fear does not happen, so the fear remains.
125526.m: Avoidance brings brief relief but keeps the fear alive.

125527.q: How does the WHO classify burnout in ICD-11?
a: As a psychosis in its own right
125527.e: In ICD-11, burnout appears as a phenomenon linked to work, not as a medical illness in its own right. It is explicitly related to chronic stress at the workplace.
125527.m: The WHO describes burnout as a result of chronic stress at work.

125528.q: Which dimension is one of Christina Maslach's three core features of burnout?
125528.e: Maslach describes emotional exhaustion, a detached attitude and reduced performance. Exhaustion is considered the central feature.
125528.m: Emotional exhaustion is a core feature of burnout.

125529.q: What is the well-known questionnaire for measuring burnout called?
125529.e: The Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) was developed by Christina Maslach and colleagues. It is used in research all over the world.
125529.m: The Maslach Burnout Inventory measures burnout.

125530.q: Which psychologist coined the term “burnout” in the 1970s?
125530.e: In the 1970s, the psychologist Herbert Freudenberger described the exhaustion of people in helping roles. In doing so, he made the term known in psychology.
125530.m: Herbert Freudenberger made the term burnout known.

125531.q: What does “depersonalisation” mean in Maslach's burnout model?
a: A detached, indifferent attitude towards others
125531.e: It means a cynical, numbed attitude towards clients, patients or colleagues. It often serves as protection against being overwhelmed further.
125531.m: With burnout, people often become detached and cynical.

125532.q: In which professions was burnout originally described above all?
125532.e: The first descriptions concerned people in nursing, social work and counselling. Today we know that burnout can occur in all professions.
125532.m: Burnout was first described in caring professions.

125533.q: According to the job demands-resources model, when does the risk of burnout rise particularly?
125533.e: The model distinguishes stressful demands from supporting resources such as freedom to make decisions or support. If resources are lacking under high strain, the risk rises.
125533.m: High strain and little support encourage burnout.

125534.q: Which measure is considered important for preventing burnout?
a: Being available on your mobile at all times
125534.e: Breaks, holidays, sleep and a clear separation of work and free time help to rebuild strength. Social support also protects.
125534.m: Recovery and clear boundaries protect against burnout.

a: Too little exercise in everyday life
125535.e: PTSD develops after a traumatic experience such as a serious accident, war, violence or a natural disaster. Not everyone who experiences a trauma develops PTSD.

125536.q: What is the sudden, unwanted reliving of a trauma as if it were happening right now called?
125536.e: In a flashback, images, sounds or feelings of the trauma come back very vividly. Experts also speak of intrusions.
125536.m: A flashback is an unwanted reliving of the trauma.

125537.q: In PTSD, what is meant by “hyperarousal”?
a: Lasting overexcitement and being easily startled
125537.e: Hyperarousal means the body is constantly on alert. Those affected sleep badly, are irritable and startle easily.
125537.m: In PTSD, the body often stays on alert.

125538.q: Which therapy method for PTSD uses targeted eye movements?
125538.e: EMDR stands for “Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing” and was developed by Francine Shapiro. Memories are processed with the help of eye movements.
125538.m: EMDR is a trauma therapy using eye movements.

125539.q: Which English term was used in the First World War for the psychological effects of war on soldiers?
125539.e: “Shell shock” refers to the shock of exploding shells. Many of the symptoms described at that time would be classed as PTSD today.
125539.m: Shell shock was an early name for war trauma.

125540.q: What is the short-term reaction directly after a trauma called, which usually fades within hours to days?
125540.e: The acute stress reaction is a normal, temporary reaction to an extreme event. If the symptoms last a long time, PTSD can develop.
125540.m: An acute stress reaction usually fades quickly.

125541.q: Which diagnosis was newly introduced in ICD-11 for the effects of long-lasting, repeated trauma?
125541.e: Complex PTSD includes the PTSD symptoms plus problems with regulating emotions, self-image and relationships. It occurs, for example, after long captivity or war.

125542.q: What is a stimulus called that triggers memories of the trauma in people with PTSD?
125542.e: A trigger can be a sound, a smell or a place that reminds the person of the trauma. Many of those affected try to avoid such stimuli.
125542.m: A trigger sets off memories of a trauma.

125543.q: Which three core symptoms characterise ADHD?
a: Sadness, lack of drive, sleep disorder
125543.e: ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Typical are problems with attention, a strong urge to move and acting impulsively.
125543.m: ADHD shows itself through inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.

125544.q: Which active substance is often used to treat ADHD with medication?
125544.e: Methylphenidate is a stimulant that strengthens the effect of messenger substances in the brain. In many people affected it improves attention and self-control.
125544.m: Methylphenidate is a common ADHD medicine.

125545.q: In which Swiss city was methylphenidate first produced by the chemical company Ciba?
125545.e: The chemist Leandro Panizzon produced the substance at Ciba in Basel. Basel is still a centre of the pharmaceutical industry today.

125546.q: What is the form of ADHD without marked hyperactivity often called in everyday language?
125546.e: In the mainly inattentive type, the strong urge to move is missing. Those affected seem more dreamy and distracted.
125546.m: ADD is a form of ADHD without strong hyperactivity.

125547.q: At what stage of life does ADHD begin?
125547.e: ADHD is a developmental disorder. The first signs appear in childhood, even if the diagnosis is sometimes only made later.

125548.q: According to current knowledge, which factor has the greatest influence on the development of ADHD?
125548.e: Twin and family studies show that ADHD is highly heritable. Environmental factors can play a part, but sugar or upbringing alone do not cause ADHD.

125549.q: Which messenger substances are particularly in the focus of ADHD research?
125549.e: In ADHD, signal transmission with dopamine and noradrenaline is altered. These messenger substances are important for attention, motivation and self-control.
125549.m: Dopamine and noradrenaline play an important role in ADHD.

125550.q: What is true of ADHD in adulthood?
125550.e: In many people affected, symptoms remain into adulthood, often in a changed form. Hyperactivity then often becomes inner restlessness.

125551.q: Which character from Heinrich Hoffmann's “Struwwelpeter” is often seen as an early portrayal of ADHD-like behaviour?
a: Augustus who would not eat his soup
125551.e: Fidgety Philip cannot sit still at the table and finally pulls the tablecloth down. That is why people sometimes speak of “Fidgety Philip syndrome”.
125551.m: Fidgety Philip is seen as an early portrayal of hyperactivity.

125552.q: In which two areas do the core features of an autism spectrum disorder show themselves?
125552.e: Autistic people often have difficulties with social interaction and communication. In addition, there are restricted interests and repeated behaviours.
125552.m: Autism affects social communication and repeated patterns of behaviour.

125553.q: Which former diagnosis was merged into autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5?
125553.e: Asperger's syndrome is named after the Austrian paediatrician Hans Asperger. Today the different forms are grouped together as a spectrum.
125553.m: Asperger's syndrome is now part of the autism spectrum.

125554.q: Which child psychiatrist described early childhood autism in the 1940s?
125554.e: In the USA, Leo Kanner published a well-known description of children with autistic features. Early childhood autism is therefore also called Kanner's syndrome.
125554.m: Leo Kanner described early childhood autism.

125555.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist introduced the term “autism” into technical language?
125555.e: Eugen Bleuler was a professor of psychiatry in Zurich and used the word in 1911. He originally meant a withdrawal into one's own inner world.
125555.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the word autism.

125556.q: What does research show about the claimed link between vaccinations and autism?
125556.e: Large studies with millions of children found no link. The study that spread this claim was withdrawn because of falsified data.

125557.q: Why do people speak of a “spectrum” today?
a: The characteristics and the need for support vary greatly
There are exactly three fixed types
125557.e: Autistic people differ greatly in language, abilities and need for support. The term spectrum reflects this variety.
125557.m: Autism shows itself in very different ways.

125558.q: What is self-stimulating, repeated behaviour such as rocking or hand-flapping called?
125558.e: Stimming helps many autistic people to calm down or process stimuli. It is usually harmless and should not simply be suppressed.
125558.m: Stimming helps autistic people regulate themselves.

125559.q: Which special feature of perception is common in autism?
a: Over- or under-sensitivity to sensory stimuli
125559.e: Many autistic people experience sounds, light or touch as very intense or hardly noticeable. Loud, crowded rooms can therefore be very stressful.
125559.m: Autistic people often perceive sensory stimuli differently.

125560.q: Which term describes the view that neurological differences such as autism are natural variations of human beings?
125560.e: The term neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains. It aims to make strengths visible and reduce exclusion.
125560.m: Neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains.

125561.e: The Viennese doctor Sigmund Freud developed psychoanalysis around 1900. It stresses the importance of unconscious processes.

125562.e: Carl Rogers put the person and their ability to grow at the centre. The therapist accompanies rather than prescribing solutions.

125563.q: According to Carl Rogers, which basic attitude is one of the core conditions of helpful therapy?
a: Rewards in the form of presents
125563.e: Rogers names empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness. These attitudes are meant to make change possible for the client.
125563.m: Empathy is a core attitude of client-centred therapy.

125564.q: What is especially at the centre of systemic therapy?
125564.e: Systemic therapy looks at problems in connection with family, partnerships or other groups. Relatives are often included in the therapy.
125564.m: Systemic therapy looks at people within their environment.

125565.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist founded analytical psychology?
125565.e: C. G. Jung worked in Zurich and coined terms such as “collective unconscious” and “archetype”. He later broke away from Freud.
125565.m: C. G. Jung founded analytical psychology.

125566.q: What changed in Switzerland with the prescription model in 2022?
a: Psychological psychotherapy is paid for by basic health insurance when prescribed by a doctor
Only doctors may hold therapy sessions
Therapy is now only available online
125566.e: Before, psychological psychotherapists had to work under a doctor's supervision for the health insurance to pay. Now, on a doctor's prescription, they can bill basic insurance independently.
125566.m: Since the prescription model, basic insurance pays for psychological psychotherapy prescribed by a doctor.

125567.q: Which factor does research consider one of the most important active factors in any psychotherapy?
a: The size of the therapy room
The length of the journey there
125567.e: A trusting relationship between client and therapist helps success across different schools of therapy. This is also called the therapeutic alliance.
125567.m: A good therapeutic relationship is central to the success of therapy.

a: Feelings from earlier relationships are directed at the therapist
Passing files on to the health insurer
125568.e: In transference, the patient unconsciously experiences the therapist in a similar way to important people from the past. These feelings are worked through in therapy.
125568.m: In transference, old relationship patterns appear in therapy.

125569.q: What distinguishes a psychiatrist from a psychologist?
a: A psychiatrist is a doctor and may prescribe medicines
A psychiatrist only works with children
A psychiatrist may not hold conversations
125569.e: Psychiatrists have studied medicine and completed specialist training. Psychologists have studied psychology and do not prescribe medicines.
125569.m: Psychiatrists are doctors and may prescribe medicines.

125570.q: What is the long-established psychiatric university hospital in Zurich called?
125570.e: The Burghölzli opened in 1870 and is now part of the Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich. In the early 20th century it was a world-famous centre of psychiatry.
125570.m: The Burghölzli is the well-known psychiatric hospital in Zurich.

125571.e: Eugen Bleuler introduced the term at the beginning of the 20th century. The word means roughly “split mind”, but it does not mean a split personality.
125571.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia.

125572.q: Which group of medicines is mainly used to treat psychoses?
125572.e: Antipsychotics, also called neuroleptics, reduce symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations. They act mainly on the dopamine system.

125573.q: Under Swiss law, what is it called when a person is placed in an institution against their will for their own protection?
125573.e: Placement for care and assistance is regulated in the Civil Code. It is only allowed if the necessary treatment or care cannot be provided in any other way.
125573.m: Placement for care and assistance is a protective measure in the Civil Code.

a: A perception without an external stimulus
125574.e: In a hallucination, someone hears, sees or feels something that is not there. Voices that other people cannot hear are common, for example.
125574.m: A hallucination is a perception without a real stimulus.

125575.q: Which substance has long been used as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder?
125575.e: Lithium salts can reduce relapses into mania and depression. Because the effective dose is close to the toxic one, the blood level is checked regularly.
125575.m: Lithium stabilises mood in bipolar disorder.

125576.q: What does a psychiatric day clinic offer?
a: Treatment during the day, nights at home
125576.e: The day clinic is a partly inpatient service. Patients spend the day at the clinic with therapies and return home in the evening.
125576.m: In a day clinic you are treated during the day and sleep at home.

a: People are looked down on and excluded because of a characteristic
People are given an award for an achievement
People receive a new identity card
125577.e: In stigmatisation, a characteristic, such as an illness, is linked with negative prejudices. As a result, those affected are put at a disadvantage.
125577.m: Stigmatisation means looking down on people because of a characteristic.

125578.q: What did the Greek word “stigma” originally mean?
a: A prick or a brand mark
125578.e: In ancient Greece, a stigma was a mark that had been burnt or cut into the skin. Today it means a characteristic for which someone is looked down on.
125578.m: A stigma was originally a brand mark.

a: Those affected turn prejudices against themselves
You register yourself with the doctor
125579.e: People who take society's prejudices to heart often feel ashamed and less valuable. This can make recovery even harder.
125579.m: In self-stigmatisation, those affected turn prejudices against themselves.

125580.q: What is a common consequence of the stigmatisation of mental illness?
a: Those affected seek help later or not at all
125580.e: Out of shame and fear of rejection, many people keep their symptoms to themselves. As a result, treatment often starts late.
125580.m: Stigma stops people from seeking help.

125581.q: According to research, which measure is particularly effective in reducing prejudice against people with mental illness?
125581.e: According to the contact hypothesis, direct encounters reduce prejudice. That is why personal accounts from those affected are often used in anti-stigma programmes.

125582.q: Which wording is considered more respectful?
125582.e: This wording puts the person before the illness. That way the person is not reduced to their diagnosis.
125582.m: Respectful language puts the person before the diagnosis.

125583.q: What is the Swiss campaign called that encourages people to talk openly about mental health?
125583.e: The campaign is a project of the German-speaking cantons and the Pro Mente Sana foundation on behalf of Health Promotion Switzerland. It gives tips on how to start conversations about mental health problems.
125583.m: The campaign “Wie geht's dir?” encourages conversations about mental health.

125584.q: What is meant by structural discrimination against people with mental illness?
a: Disadvantage caused by rules and institutions
125584.e: Structural discrimination comes from laws, procedures or the way resources are shared out, not from individual prejudices. One example is poorer care compared with physical illnesses.
125584.m: Structural discrimination is built into rules and institutions.

125585.q: What can children and young people contact the Pro Juventute 147 helpline about?
125585.e: The 147 helpline is open for any topic, such as stress, bullying, family or worries about the future. No worry is too small.
125585.m: You can talk about any worry on 147.

125586.q: When can you reach the 147 helpline?
125586.e: The 147 helpline can be reached around the clock, 365 days a year. That way, young people can find support at night too.
125586.m: The 147 helpline is available day and night.

125587.q: How much does a call to the 147 helpline cost?
a: A flat rate of ten francs
It varies from canton to canton
125587.e: The helpline is free for children and young people. That way no one has to go without help for lack of money.

125588.q: Apart from by phone, how else can you reach the 147 helpline?
a: By text message, chat and email
Only in person at a counter
125588.e: Besides the phone, advice is available by text message, in a chat and by email. Many young people prefer writing to calling.
125588.m: The 147 helpline can also be reached by text, chat and email.

125589.q: What is true of conversations with the 147 helpline?
125589.e: The advice is confidential, and you do not have to give your name. This makes it easier to talk about difficult topics too.
125589.m: On 147 you can talk about your worries in confidence.

125590.q: What kind of organisation is Pro Juventute?
a: A Swiss foundation for children and young people
125590.e: Pro Juventute is a non-profit foundation. It supports children, young people and parents with advice and projects.
125590.m: Pro Juventute is a foundation for children and young people.

125591.q: What is the phone number of Die Dargebotene Hand, the Swiss helpline for adults?
125591.e: Die Dargebotene Hand can be reached on 143 and is mainly for adults. The number 145 belongs to Tox Info, 118 to the fire brigade.
125591.m: Die Dargebotene Hand has the number 143.

125592.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance service when a life is in acute danger?
125592.e: In a medical emergency such as an acute danger to life, you call the ambulance service on 144. The 147 helpline is for talking about worries, and 145 is the number of Tox Info.
125592.m: When a life is in acute danger, you dial 144.

125593.q: Which American psychiatrist is regarded as the founder of cognitive therapy?
125593.e: Aaron T. Beck first developed cognitive therapy for depression. He showed how negative thought patterns influence feelings.
125593.m: Aaron T. Beck founded cognitive therapy.

125594.q: Who developed rational emotive behaviour therapy?
125594.e: Albert Ellis believed that irrational beliefs cause distressing feelings. His method is one of the roots of cognitive behavioural therapy.
125594.m: Albert Ellis developed rational emotive behaviour therapy.

125595.q: What does Beck's cognitive triad refer to?
a: A negative view of yourself, the world and the future
125595.e: Beck described a negative view of oneself, one's surroundings and the future in depression. The therapy examines these thoughts together.
125595.m: The cognitive triad is a negative view of yourself, the world and the future.

125596.q: What is the thinking error called in which you conclude the worst possible outcome from a small problem?
125596.e: In catastrophising, one mistake immediately becomes total failure. Therapy helps to find more realistic thoughts.
125596.m: Catastrophising turns small things into disasters.

125597.q: What does the “B” stand for in Albert Ellis's ABC model?
125597.e: A is the activating event, B the belief and C the consequence. It is not the event alone but how it is judged that determines the feeling.
125597.m: In the ABC model, how an event is judged determines the feeling.

125598.q: What is the technique called in which unhelpful thoughts are recognised, checked and replaced with more helpful ones?
125598.e: In cognitive restructuring, you look for evidence for and against a thought. This leads to more balanced views.

125599.q: What is the aim of behavioural activation in depression?
a: Staying in bed as much as possible
125599.e: Depressed people often withdraw, which lowers their mood further. Planned, positive activities break this cycle.
125599.m: Behavioural activation gets mood going again through activity.

125600.q: What is the thinking error called in which only extremes such as “perfect” or “total failure” are seen?
125600.e: In black-and-white thinking, there are no shades in between. Anyone who is not perfect then sees themselves straight away as a failure.
125600.m: Black-and-white thinking has no shades in between.

125601.q: Which skill do people practise in many modern behavioural therapies by perceiving the moment consciously and without judging it?
125601.e: Mindfulness is a core element of newer methods such as Marsha Linehan's dialectical behaviour therapy. You learn to notice thoughts and feelings without reacting to them straight away.
125601.m: Mindfulness means experiencing the moment consciously and without judging.

a: The interaction between mind and body
125602.e: The term is made up of the Greek “psyche” (soul) and “soma” (body). Psychosomatics studies how mental factors influence physical complaints and the other way round.
125602.m: Psychosomatics studies the interplay between mind and body.

125603.q: Which model explains illness as the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors?
125603.e: The biopsychosocial model was made known by the psychiatrist George Engel. It adds the mind and the environment to the purely biological view.
125603.m: The biopsychosocial model connects body, mind and social environment.

125604.q: Which hormone does the adrenal cortex release in larger amounts during lasting stress?
125604.e: Cortisol provides energy and helps to cope with strain. If it stays high for a long time, it can weaken the immune system and disturb sleep.
125604.m: Cortisol is an important stress hormone.

a: Physical complaints without a sufficient physical cause being found
A broken bone after a fall
A heart disease present from birth
125605.e: Those affected really suffer from pain or other complaints, but the examinations do not explain them sufficiently. The complaints are not imagined.
125605.m: In somatoform disorders, real complaints have no sufficient physical cause.

125606.q: Which complaint is particularly often partly caused by stress and tension?
125606.e: Under stress, the neck and head muscles tense up. This can trigger a pressing headache.

125607.q: What is the effect called that arises solely from positive expectations of a treatment?
125607.e: Just expecting a remedy to help can measurably relieve complaints. Placebo means “I shall please” in Latin.
125607.m: The placebo effect comes from positive expectations.

125608.q: What is the effect called in which negative expectations cause or worsen complaints?
125608.e: People who expect side effects, for example, feel them more often, even with a dummy pill. Nocebo means “I shall harm” in Latin.
125608.m: Negative expectations can trigger complaints through the nocebo effect.

125609.q: Which researcher shaped the modern concept of stress with the “general adaptation syndrome”?
125609.e: Hans Selye described how the body reacts to lasting strain in phases: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. He made the term stress known in medicine.
125609.m: Hans Selye shaped the modern understanding of stress.

125907.q: Where do you stick the AED pads on adults in the standard position?
a: Below the right collarbone and on the left side of the chest
Both pads next to each other on the breastbone
One on the stomach and one on the lower back
One pad on each upper arm
125907.e: This way the current flows diagonally through the heart. The devices also show the position on the pads with a picture.
125907.m: The AED pads place the heart between them.

125908.q: In ventricular fibrillation without defibrillation, roughly how does the chance of survival change per minute?
a: It falls by about 7 to 10 per cent
It stays the same for the first 10 minutes
It falls by about 50 per cent
125908.e: Without treatment, the chance of survival drops considerably every minute. Chest compressions slow this loss but do not replace the shock.
125908.m: In ventricular fibrillation, every minute until the first shock counts.

125909.q: What do you pay attention to when sticking AED pads on a person with an implanted pacemaker?
a: Do not stick the pad directly over the device
Switch off the pacemaker first with a magnet
Do not use the AED at all
Stick the pads on the back
125909.e: A pacemaker usually lies below the left or right collarbone and can be felt as a bulge. The pad is stuck next to it, a few centimetres away.
125909.m: A pacemaker is no reason not to use the AED.

125910.q: What should you do if a person's chest is wet before you stick on the AED pads?
a: Moisten the pads with water as well
Choose a shock with double the energy
Stick the pads on the clothes
125910.e: On wet skin the pads stick poorly and the current can flow away over the surface. A quick dry is enough.
125910.m: The AED pads always go on dry, bare skin.

125911.q: Why must nobody touch the person while the AED is analysing and delivering a shock?
a: Movements disturb the analysis and the current can hit the helpers
Because otherwise the battery runs flat
Because otherwise the device changes language
Because the pads would then fall off
125911.e: The AED must be able to measure the heart rhythm without disturbance. During the shock, the current could also jump to the helpers.
125911.m: During analysis and shock, nobody touches the person.

125912.q: What do helpers do immediately after an AED shock?
a: Carry on with chest compressions at once
Feel for the pulse for one minute
Put the person in the recovery position
125912.e: Even after a successful shock, the heart often does not yet pump enough. That is why compressions continue straight away until the device announces the next analysis.
125912.m: After the shock, compressions continue without a break.

125913.q: How should gasping breaths in an unconscious person be interpreted?
a: As a sign of cardiac arrest
As a sign of normal recovery
As a sign of deep sleep
125913.e: Gasping consists of rare, slow breaths without effective gas exchange. It does not count as normal breathing, so you start resuscitation immediately.
125913.m: Gasping is not normal breathing and calls for immediate chest compressions.

125914.q: According to the ERC guidelines, with how many rescue breaths do you begin resuscitating a child?
125914.e: In children, cardiac arrest is usually the result of a lack of oxygen. That is why they first receive oxygen through five rescue breaths.
125914.m: In children, resuscitation starts with five rescue breaths.

125915.q: Which medicine does the ambulance service give as standard during resuscitation?
125915.e: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and so increases the pressure with which blood flows to the heart and brain. It is injected into a vein or into the bone.
125915.m: Adrenaline is the most important medicine in resuscitation.

125916.q: What is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in adults?
125916.e: Narrowed coronary arteries and heart attacks often lead to ventricular fibrillation. This rhythm suddenly stops the heart's pumping.
125916.m: Sudden cardiac death is usually caused by a disease of the coronary arteries.

125917.q: In the classic chain of rescue, which link comes directly after the emergency call?
125917.e: Several minutes often pass between the alarm and the arrival of the professionals. Laypeople bridge this time with first aid.
125917.m: After the emergency call, helpers give first aid until the ambulance service arrives.

125918.q: How many links does the European Resuscitation Council's chain of survival have?
125918.e: The links are early recognition and emergency call, early chest compressions, early defibrillation and further treatment by professionals. Each link increases the chance of survival.
125918.m: The chain of survival in cardiac arrest has four links.

a: Several injuries at the same time, of which one or their combination is life-threatening
A single minor injury on several days
A chronic disease of several organs
125919.e: In polytrauma, several regions of the body or organ systems are injured. What matters is that the injuries together threaten life.
125919.m: Polytrauma is a life-threatening multiple injury.

125920.q: Where does the ambulance service in Switzerland take polytrauma patients whenever possible?
a: Always to the nearest regional hospital
125920.e: Severely injured people are treated in a few large centres where all specialities are available around the clock. A longer transport, for example by helicopter, is accepted for this.
125920.m: Severely injured people belong in a trauma centre.

125921.q: Which three conditions form the so-called lethal triad in a severely injured patient?
a: Hypothermia, acidosis and a clotting disorder
High blood pressure, diabetes and being overweight
125921.e: Hypothermia and acidification of the blood make blood clotting worse. As a result the patient bleeds more, which makes the other two conditions even worse.
125921.m: Hypothermia, acidosis and clotting disorders make each other worse in severely injured people.

125922.q: What does the term “golden hour” mean in trauma care?
a: The first hour after the accident, in which quick treatment achieves a particularly great deal
The hour before sunset with good visibility for helicopters
The time when operations are cheapest
The first hour of rest after an operation
125922.e: The term stresses that severely injured people should reach a suitable hospital as quickly as possible. The exact length is more of a guiding idea than a fixed limit.
125922.m: For severely injured people, the time until final treatment is what counts most.

125923.q: What does the “B” stand for in the ABCDE approach of emergency medicine?
125923.e: The approach checks, in order, the airway, breathing, circulation, neurological state and the undressed body. What kills fastest is treated first.
125923.m: In the ABCDE approach, breathing comes straight after the airway.

125924.q: Why does the ambulance service put a pelvic binder on an accident victim?
a: To reduce internal bleeding if a broken pelvis is suspected
To support the spine when lifting
125924.e: With an unstable pelvic fracture, a lot of blood can be lost inside the pelvis. The binder presses the bones together and reduces the space for bleeding.
125924.m: A pelvic binder stabilises the pelvis and slows internal bleeding.

125925.q: What is the aim of “damage control surgery” in severely injured people?
a: First only control bleeding and contamination, with the final repair following later
Fully repair all injuries at once in one long operation
125925.e: A long operation would overwhelm the weakened body. After a short emergency operation, the patient is stabilised in intensive care and the surgery is completed later.
125925.m: In severely injured people, life is saved first with a short operation, and everything is repaired later.

125926.q: How do you position a person with anaphylaxis who is mainly short of breath but conscious?
a: Sitting or with the upper body raised
Head down with the feet raised
125926.e: Breathing is easier when sitting, because the breathing muscles work better. If the circulation is weak, however, you lay the person flat.
125926.m: If someone is short of breath, let them sit upright.

125927.q: In an allergic reaction, which signs point to life-threatening anaphylaxis?
a: Shortness of breath and circulatory weakness
Slight redness at the sting site
125927.e: In anaphylaxis, not only the skin but also the airways and circulation are affected. Then an immediate call to 144 is needed.
125927.m: Shortness of breath and circulation problems turn an allergy into an emergency.

125928.q: In which period is the chance of survival highest for avalanche victims who are completely buried?
a: On the day after the avalanche
125928.e: Most buried people survive the first few minutes. After that the survival curve drops steeply, because many run out of air.
125928.m: In an avalanche, quick rescue in the first few minutes is what counts.

125929.q: What do most avalanche victims who are recovered dead after a short time die of?
125929.e: Once it stops moving, the snow packs down like concrete and blocks the mouth and nose. Without an air space, a lack of oxygen sets in quickly.
125929.m: The greatest danger under an avalanche is suffocation.

125930.q: Why do all avalanche transceivers send on the same frequency?
a: So that every device can locate every other one
So that they use less power
So that they do not interfere with mobile phones
So that they can also be used as radios
125930.e: All avalanche transceivers work internationally on 457 kilohertz. This way, any device can find a buried person, no matter which brand they are wearing.
125930.m: All avalanche transceivers work on the same frequency.

125931.q: Which emergency equipment is standard on ski tours away from secured pistes?
a: Avalanche transceiver, avalanche shovel and avalanche probe
Foil blanket, mobile phone and map
125931.e: With the transceiver you locate the buried person, with the probe you confirm their position and with the shovel you dig them out. If any one of these is missing, the rescue takes much longer.
125931.m: Transceiver, shovel and probe always belong together.

125932.q: Why is rescue by companions so crucial in avalanche accidents?
a: Because it is much faster than an organised rescue on the spot
Because it is cheaper than a helicopter mission
Because rescue services are not allowed to fly into the mountains
Because only companions know the victims
125932.e: Even a helicopter usually needs much longer for the alarm and the flight than the first critical minutes. The companions are already there.
125932.m: In avalanches, it is often the companions who save the lives of those buried.

125933.q: What do you uncover as early as possible when recovering an avalanche victim?
a: The head with the mouth and nose
125933.e: As soon as the airway is clear, the person can breathe. During the rescue, you also look out for a possible air pocket in front of the face.
125933.m: With avalanche victims, the head and airway are uncovered first.

125934.q: Below which core body temperature is it called hypothermia?
125934.e: The normal core temperature is about 37 degrees. If it falls below 35 degrees, a person is considered hypothermic.
125934.m: Hypothermia begins below a core temperature of 35 degrees.

125935.q: According to the Swiss staging system, what characterises stage I hypothermia?
125935.e: In the first stage, the person is awake and shivers strongly. Shivering produces heat and is a protective mechanism.
125935.m: Someone who is shivering strongly and thinking clearly is mildly hypothermic.

125936.q: Below roughly which core temperature does shivering usually stop?
125936.e: As the body cools further, the energy reserves run out and the muscles no longer work effectively. A lack of shivering is therefore a warning sign.
125936.m: If a hypothermic person stops shivering, it becomes dangerous.

125937.q: Why do you move a severely hypothermic person as gently as possible and keep them horizontal?
a: Because otherwise ventricular fibrillation can be triggered
Because otherwise they fall asleep immediately
125937.e: The cold heart is very easily irritated. Jerky movements and cold blood from the limbs can trigger a dangerous rhythm.
125937.m: Hypothermic people are kept still and lying flat.

125938.q: What does the saying “Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead” mean?
a: That you keep resuscitating hypothermic people without signs of life
That the dead must always be warmed up
That you only resuscitate in summer
125938.e: Cold greatly reduces the brain's need for oxygen. That is why even people with a long cardiac arrest in deep hypothermia have a chance of survival.
125938.m: In severe hypothermia, resuscitation is not given up too soon.

125939.q: How is a deeply hypothermic person in cardiac arrest most effectively rewarmed in hospital?
a: With a heart-lung machine or ECMO
With warm tea through a stomach tube
With infrared lamps on the skin
125939.e: In extracorporeal rewarming, the blood is warmed outside the body and enriched with oxygen. At the same time, the machine takes over the pumping work of the heart.
125939.m: In hypothermia with cardiac arrest, a heart-lung machine helps.

125940.q: Why do small children cool down faster than adults?
a: Because their body surface is larger in relation to their volume
Because their heart beats more slowly
125940.e: The body loses heat through its surface, while heat is produced and stored in its volume. A small body has relatively a lot of surface and therefore loses heat quickly.
125940.m: Small children need especially good protection from the cold.

125941.q: Why does alcohol increase the risk of hypothermia?
a: Because it widens the blood vessels in the skin, so more heat is lost
Because it heats the body up strongly from inside
125941.e: The feeling of warmth on the skin is deceptive, because heat flows out through the widened vessels. Alcohol also clouds your judgement of the danger.
125941.m: Alcohol only seems to warm you and in fact encourages cooling down.

125942.q: Which language does the word “triage” come from?
125942.e: The verb “trier” means to sort or select. In German medical services it is also called “Sichtung”.
125942.m: Triage means sorting patients by urgency.

125943.q: Which of Napoleon's military surgeons is regarded as the founder of modern triage?
125943.e: Larrey had the wounded treated according to how serious their injuries were and not according to rank. He also introduced fast transport carts for the wounded.
125943.m: Modern triage goes back to Napoleon's surgeon Larrey.

125944.q: What does the colour red mean in triage after a major incident?
125944.e: People marked red are acutely life-threateningly injured but have a good chance of survival with immediate help. Yellow stands for urgent cases, green for minor ones.
125944.m: In triage, red means treat immediately.

125945.q: In the START system, which category do all people who can walk on their own receive?
125945.e: People who can walk usually have no immediately life-threatening injury. They are sent to a gathering point and assessed more closely later.
125945.m: In the START system, people who can walk are first considered slightly injured.

125946.q: After a major incident, an injured person is breathing more than 30 times a minute. Which category do you put them in under the START system?
125946.e: Very fast breathing shows a serious disturbance of breathing or circulation. Such people need help immediately.
125946.m: If an injured person breathes very fast, they must be treated immediately.

125947.q: Above which capillary refill time is a person considered critical in the START system?
125947.e: You press on a fingernail bed and measure how quickly it turns pink again. Slow refilling points to shock.
125947.m: A slow return of colour to the nail bed points to shock.

125948.q: What does the Manchester Triage System in the emergency department set for each level of urgency?
a: A maximum waiting time until first seeing a doctor
125948.e: The system divides patients into five colour levels. Red means immediately, blue may wait the longest.
125948.m: The Manchester Triage System works with five colour levels.

125949.q: What does the German abbreviation MANV stand for in emergency services?
125949.e: A mass casualty incident occurs when there are more injured people than available rescue resources. Triage then becomes the central task of the first emergency teams.
125949.m: In a mass casualty incident, triage is essential.

125950.q: In which city is Tox Info Suisse based?
125950.e: The centre works closely with the University of Zurich. From there it gives advice to the whole of Switzerland.
125950.m: Tox Info Suisse is based in Zurich.

125951.q: When can the Tox Info Suisse emergency number be reached?
a: Only on weekdays during office hours
125951.e: Poisonings happen at any time of day. That is why experts answer the calls without a break.
125951.m: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night.

125952.q: Which age group among children is most often affected in poisoning enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
125952.e: Toddlers explore their surroundings with their mouths. That is why they often swallow household products, parts of plants or medicines.
125952.m: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept out of reach of toddlers.

125953.q: What should you not do if a child has swallowed a corrosive cleaning product?
125953.e: When vomiting, the corrosive liquid would damage the oesophagus a second time. It could also get into the lungs.
125953.m: After swallowing cleaning products, never make someone vomit yourself.

125954.q: Which group of products is most often involved in enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
125954.e: Medicines are found in almost every household and get mixed up, taken in too high a dose or found by children. Household products come next.
125954.m: Most poisoning enquiries are about medicines.

125955.q: What should you have ready if possible when calling Tox Info Suisse?
125955.e: The packaging shows the name and the ingredients. This lets the expert assess the risk accurately.
125955.m: In a poisoning, keep the product's packaging ready.

125956.q: Which remedy is used in many poisonings to bind toxic substances in the gut?
125956.e: Activated charcoal has a huge inner surface to which many substances stick. An expert decides whether it makes sense to use it.
125956.m: Activated charcoal binds many poisons before they enter the blood.

125957.q: How is the Swiss Samaritan Association organised at grassroots level?
125957.e: The clubs work largely on a voluntary basis and are grouped into cantonal associations. They offer courses and first aid services in their region.
125957.m: Samaritan work depends on local clubs with volunteers.

125958.q: Which course must people in Switzerland have attended before applying for a learner's permit for driving a car?
a: The first aid for children course
125958.e: The emergency first aid course teaches how to behave at the scene of an accident, positioning and chest compressions. Providers include the Samaritan clubs.
125958.m: Anyone who wants to learn to drive first attends the emergency first aid course.

125959.q: What role does the Interverband für Rettungswesen (IVR) play in Switzerland?
a: It is the umbrella association for rescue services
It is the police emergency call centre
It is a private ambulance company
It is the Federal Office for Civil Protection
125959.e: In the IVR, organisations and experts from the rescue services work together. It campaigns for a uniform quality of rescue.
125959.m: The IVR is the umbrella association of Swiss rescue services.

125960.q: What is the Interverband für Rettungswesen called in French?
125960.e: The French abbreviation is IAS. In French-speaking Switzerland the association is known by this name.
125960.m: In French-speaking Switzerland, the IVR is called Interassociation de sauvetage.

125961.q: What does the IVR award to ambulance services that meet its quality guidelines?
125961.e: Ambulance services are checked for equipment, staff and procedures. The recognition shows that they meet the Swiss-wide standards.
125961.m: Ambulance services recognised by the IVR meet uniform quality standards.

125962.q: Besides ambulance services, which facilities are also recognised according to IVR guidelines?
125962.e: The emergency call centres take calls, send out rescue resources and guide laypeople over the phone. Uniform quality requirements apply to them too.
125962.m: The 144 emergency call centres also follow Swiss-wide guidelines.

125963.q: At which level of education are paramedics trained in Switzerland?
a: At a college of higher education (Höhere Fachschule)
125963.e: The qualification is called qualified paramedic HF. The training combines college and practical work in the ambulance service.
125963.m: In Switzerland, paramedics are trained at colleges of higher education.

125964.q: Which qualification do patient transport attendants earn in Switzerland?
a: A federal diploma of higher vocational education
A course certificate from the employer
125964.e: The professional examination leads to the federal diploma. Patient transport attendants mainly work on planned and less urgent patient transports.
125964.m: Patient transport attendants qualify with a federal diploma.

125965.q: Which target for response time do the IVR guidelines set for ambulance services?
a: On the scene within 15 minutes in 90 per cent of call-outs
On the scene within 2 minutes in all call-outs
Within 1 hour in 50 per cent of call-outs
125965.e: The response time is the time it takes for the ambulance service to reach the scene. It is an important figure for planning ambulance stations.
125965.m: Ambulance services should reach most emergencies within a quarter of an hour.

125966.q: When is a tourniquet used in first aid?
a: For life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that cannot be stopped any other way
For every small cut on a finger
For a bruise without a wound
125966.e: A tourniquet stops the blood flow to the whole limb. It is the right tool when pressure and a pressure bandage are not enough or there is no time for them.
125966.m: A tourniquet is meant for life-threatening bleeding from arms and legs.

125967.q: Where is a tourniquet applied when the wound is known?
a: A few centimetres above the wound, towards the body, not over a joint
Below the wound, towards the hand or foot
125967.e: Above the wound, it cuts off the supply to the bleeding site. Over a joint, the blood vessel cannot be reliably compressed.
125967.m: The tourniquet goes above the wound and never on a joint.

125968.q: What must always be written down after applying a tourniquet?
a: The skin colour of the helper
125968.e: How long the limb has been tied off is important for treatment in hospital. The time is often written directly on the tourniquet or on the person's forehead.
125968.m: With a tourniquet, the time is always written down.

125969.q: What is the turning rod called that is used to tighten a modern tourniquet?
125969.e: Turning the rod tightens the band so much that the artery is compressed. The rod is then secured in a holder.
125969.m: A tourniquet is tightened with a turning rod called a windlass.

125970.q: Who is allowed to loosen a tourniquet once it has been applied?
a: Anyone, as soon as the bleeding has stopped
Nobody, it stays on until healing is complete
125970.e: When it is loosened, the bleeding can start again and toxic substances from the limb get into the circulation. That is why professionals decide.
125970.m: Only professionals loosen a tourniquet once it has been applied.

125971.q: Where do you apply a tourniquet if the exact source of bleeding cannot be seen?
a: As high up the limb as possible, close to the body
Exactly in the middle of the limb
125971.e: Following the principle “high and tight”, this covers all possible bleeding sites below it. Later, professionals can place the tourniquet more precisely.
125971.m: If the source of bleeding is unclear, the tourniquet goes high and tight on the limb.

125972.q: How can you tell that a tourniquet is tight enough?
a: The bleeding stops and no pulse can be felt below it
The skin below turns red and warm
The injured person feels no pain
The band can still be moved easily
125972.e: A tourniquet that is too loose only traps blood in the veins and can even make the bleeding worse. It must completely cut off the flow through the arteries.
125972.m: A tourniquet is only right when the bleeding really stops.

125973.q: Why is a thin cord unsuitable as an improvised tourniquet?
a: It cuts in and damages skin and nerves
125973.e: A narrow band puts the pressure on a small area. It injures the tissue underneath and often still does not fully compress the artery.
125973.m: A tourniquet needs a wide band, not a thin cord.

125974.q: Roughly how long is a correctly applied tourniquet considered acceptable without serious damage being expected?
125974.e: After that, the risk of muscle and nerve damage rises considerably. That is why quick transport to hospital is important.
125974.m: A tourniquet is only a stopgap until treatment in hospital.

125975.q: With which heart finding does an AED not deliver a shock?
125975.e: In asystole, there is no electrical activity at all that a shock could reorganise. Only chest compressions and medicines help here.
125975.m: A flat line cannot be treated with an electric shock.

125976.q: What do you do with a medicine patch that is stuck where an AED pad needs to go?
a: Remove it and wipe the skin
Stick the pad directly over it
125976.e: A patch under the pad can block the flow of current and cause burns. It only takes seconds to pull it off.
125976.m: No patch may be stuck under an AED pad.

125977.q: What do special child pads or a child mode on an AED do?
a: They extend the analysis time to ten minutes
They switch off the voice prompts
They deliver several shocks at the same time
125977.e: Children need a smaller amount of current than adults. If there are no child pads, the adult pads are used anyway.
125977.m: On a child, an AED may be used with reduced energy.

125978.q: How often should several helpers ideally take turns doing chest compressions?
125978.e: Chest compressions are tiring, and the depth of the compressions drops unnoticed as you tire. The changeover should happen with as short a pause as possible.
125978.m: Helpers take turns regularly during chest compressions.

125979.q: What is the longest that checking an unconscious person's breathing should take?
125979.e: You tilt the head back and look, listen and feel for breathing movements, breathing sounds and airflow. If you are unsure, you start chest compressions.
125979.m: Checking breathing takes no longer than ten seconds.

125980.q: Roughly what proportion of normal heart output does good chest compression achieve?
a: About a quarter to a third
125980.e: Chest compressions only partly replace the heart's pumping. But this is enough to supply the brain and heart with some oxygen for a while.
125980.m: Chest compressions keep an emergency circulation going until the heart beats again.

125981.q: During resuscitation, how can you tell that the heart is beating on its own again?
a: A pulse and normal breathing return
125981.e: When the heart beats by itself again, a pulse can be felt and the person often starts breathing normally again. Experts call this return of spontaneous circulation.
125981.m: When pulse and breathing return, the heart is beating on its own again.

125982.q: After successful resuscitation, what is deliberately avoided in intensive care during the first few days?
125982.e: A raised body temperature makes brain damage after a lack of oxygen worse. That is why the temperature is monitored and carefully controlled.
125982.m: After resuscitation, a controlled body temperature protects the brain.

125983.q: What does the classic chain of rescue start with?
a: The arrival of the emergency doctor
125983.e: Immediate measures include securing the scene of the accident, rescuing people from the danger zone and chest compressions. They are carried out by the first people on the scene.
125983.m: The chain of rescue begins with the people who are first at the scene.

125984.q: What is it called when the emergency call centre guides laypeople through chest compressions over the phone?
125984.e: The dispatcher counts out the rhythm and gives instructions. As a result, many more laypeople start resuscitation.
125984.m: In cardiac arrest, the emergency call centre helps with resuscitation over the phone.

125985.q: What is the job of first responders, who are alerted by smartphone app in many cantons?
a: They start resuscitation before the ambulance service arrives
They replace the emergency doctor in hospital
They direct traffic at the scene of the accident
125985.e: Volunteers trained in resuscitation who are nearby are called out at the same time as the ambulance service. They are often on the scene faster.
125985.m: In cardiac arrest, first responders bridge the time until the ambulance service arrives.

125986.q: At least how far away do you set up the warning triangle on Swiss motorways?
125986.e: Because of the high speeds, vehicles behind need a long braking distance. On other roads, 50 metres is usually enough.
125986.m: On the motorway, the warning triangle stands at least 100 metres before the accident.

125987.q: What is the top priority for helpers at the scene of an accident?
125987.e: Anyone who puts themselves in danger can become an additional victim and can no longer help anyone. That is why you first secure the scene and watch out for traffic, fire or electricity.
125987.m: Anyone who helps protects themselves first.

125988.q: Which grip do you use to quickly pull an unconscious person out of a danger zone, for example out of a car?
125988.e: You reach under the armpits, grab one of the person's forearms and pull them out of the danger zone on your own thighs. The grip is named after the Austrian Franz Rautek.
125988.m: With the Rautek manoeuvre, even a weaker person can rescue someone who is unconscious.

125989.q: What do you do with an unconscious motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet?
a: Just close the visor with tape
Bend the head with the helmet sharply forwards
125989.e: With the helmet on, the airway cannot be checked and kept clear. If possible two people remove it, stabilising the head and neck at the same time.
125989.m: If a motorcyclist is unconscious, the helmet is removed.

125990.q: Which life-threatening chest injury is relieved in an emergency with a needle?
125990.e: In a tension pneumothorax, air collects under pressure in the chest and squeezes the lungs and heart. The needle lets the air escape and buys time until a drain is inserted.
125990.m: A tension pneumothorax must be relieved immediately.

125991.q: Where do you inject an adrenaline auto-injector in anaphylaxis?
a: Into the outer side of the thigh
Into a vein on the back of the hand
Under the skin of the stomach
Into the crook of the arm
125991.e: The large thigh muscle has a good blood supply and is easy to reach. In an emergency you can even inject through trousers.
125991.m: The adrenaline pen is placed on the outer thigh.

125992.q: What do you do if anaphylaxis does not improve about 5 minutes after the first dose of adrenaline?
a: Give a second dose of adrenaline
Give the person a glass of milk
Leave the person to rest alone
125992.e: That is why many people with allergies carry two auto-injectors. The second dose is given into the other thigh.
125992.m: If the first dose of adrenaline does not help, a second one follows.

125993.q: What is anaphylaxis called that only occurs when someone does sport after eating a particular food?
125993.e: Only the combination of the food and physical exertion triggers the reaction. A well-known trigger is wheat.
125993.m: Some types of anaphylaxis also need physical exertion as a trigger.

125994.q: Which foods particularly often trigger anaphylaxis in children?
125994.e: Nuts are among the most common triggers of severe allergic reactions. Even tiny traces can be enough.
125994.m: Nuts are common triggers of anaphylaxis.

125995.q: Why does a person in anaphylactic shock quickly need a lot of intravenous fluid?
a: Because fluid leaks out of the leaky blood vessels into the tissue
